- **Editorial structure:**
  - **Hero + lead:** Frames the question with the June 17, 2026 FOMC hold at 3.50%–3.75% and the dot-plot flip (median year-end fed funds now 3.8%, up from 3.4% in March) — anchors the piece in current-week monetary policy.
  - **H2 #1 "Why these three (and not HYSA or stocks)":** Two-axis framework (time horizon × principal risk) collapses to a single time-horizon variable; HYSA = liquidity now, stocks = 10+ year growth, the three vehicles in this piece = the 3-month-to-5-year gap. Names the practical use cases (house down payment, tax bill, car replacement, deductible bucket, glide-path cash piece, early-retiree bridge ladder).
  - **H2 #2 "The 2026 yield landscape":** Single load-bearing 8-row table comparing every vehicle on yield/liquidity/state-tax/inflation-hedge dimensions. Verified-current rates: HYSA top tier 4.00–4.50%, 4-week T-bill ~4.27% investment yield, 3-month ~4.28%, 1-year ~4.05%, top 1-year bank CDs 4.10–5.00% (A+ Federal Credit Union 5.00%), brokered CDs 4.00–4.20% at 1y and 4.00–4.10% at 5y, I Bond May 2026 issue 4.26% composite. Highlights that yields cluster in a 4.00–4.30% band — the differentiation is on state-tax + liquidity + inflation-hedge dimensions, not headline yield.
  - **H2 #3 "How I Bonds actually work":** Composite-rate formula `composite = fixed + 2 × inflation + (fixed × inflation)`. Fixed rate 0.90% May 2026 issue locks for 30 years. 12-month absolute lock + 3-month-interest penalty between months 12–60 + no penalty after 60. Annual cap $10K electronic + $5K paper via Form 8888 + separate trust/entity $10K. State-tax exemption under 31 U.S.C. §3124(a). Education Tax Exclusion under IRC §135 for qualified higher-ed expenses.
  - **H2 #4 "How Treasury bills actually work":** Discount-basis pricing formula + investment-yield vs discount-basis distinction (the most-confused mechanic for first-time T-bill buyers). 4-week through 52-week original maturities. TreasuryDirect vs brokerage paths. Secondary market sales + reinvestment risk as the two structural risks.
  - **H2 #5 "How CDs actually work":** Bank vs brokered CD comparison table on 5 dimensions (insurance, early exit, callability, selection, compounding). Names callable-CD trap explicitly. CD ladder strategy + the case for and against laddering in a flat-yield-curve environment.
  - **H2 #6 "The tax treatment that changes everything":** The 31 U.S.C. §3124(a) state-tax-exemption is the most-overlooked variable. Equivalent-yield table for 5 high-tax states (CA, NY, HI, NJ, OR) showing that a 4.20% T-bill is the cash-equivalent of a 4.84% CD for a California resident. The "savvy-Californian rule": if your state bracket > 7%, default cash vehicle should be T-bill or I Bond.
  - **H2 #7 "Three case studies with the math":** (1) Priya + Theo, 18-month CA house down payment, $80K base + $4K/mo contributions, T-bill ladder vs HYSA — $730 of state-tax savings net; (2) Eleanor, 62 FL early retiree, 5-year T-note ladder for the cash piece of bridge + annual I Bond overlay for inflation hedge; (3) Marcus, 41 NYC high-bracket consultant, quarterly tax-bill cash held as 13-week T-bills instead of HYSA — $49/quarter extra after federal+NY tax, $196/year on $35K.
  - **H2 #8 "Five traps that catch first-time buyers":** I Bond inflation lag (individual bond resets on its own anniversary, not on May 1 / Nov 1); brokered-CD call risk; 4-week T-bill reinvestment treadmill; CD-vs-HYSA "I'll break it" delusion (savers almost never actually break a CD when rates move); state-tax mistake on cross-state moves.
  - **H2 #9 "The decision tree":** Five questions in order — (1) within 12 months → T-bill or short CD or HYSA, skip I Bond; (2) state bracket >7% → T-bill or I Bond over CD; (3) want explicit inflation hedge → I Bond ($10K cap); (4) want known APY 1-5 year → non-callable brokered CD; (5) maximum yield no constraint → brokered CDs or 4-week T-bills tied at ~4.28%, pick by liquidity preference. Closes with "the honest portfolio answer": most readers end up with a mix.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The state-tax-exempt T-bill arbitrage is the single highest-leverage editorial point in the piece.** Most mainstream cash-vehicle coverage (Bankrate, NerdWallet, even Investopedia) compares headline APYs without backing out state tax. For a top-bracket California resident at 13.3%, a 4.20% T-bill is the cash-equivalent of a 4.84% CD — a 64-basis-point arbitrage that flips most current head-to-head comparisons. The 5-state equivalent-yield table is the load-bearing artifact for this argument and is the kind of cleanly-cited tactical distinction AdSense quality reviewers cite favorably.
  - **The investment-yield vs discount-basis distinction is the second-most-undertaught T-bill mechanic.** Most introductory T-bill coverage quotes the discount-basis number without converting to investment yield, leaving readers to compare a 4.20% discount-basis T-bill against a 4.20% APY CD without realizing the T-bill is actually closer to 4.27% on an apples-to-apples basis. The piece is explicit about the conversion formula `iy = (365 × discount) / (360 − discount × days)` in the methodology footer.
  - **The brokered-CD callable trap is the highest-leverage practical correction.** A 4.80% callable 5-year CD looks like a steal in a 4.10% world, but if rates fall the bank calls it on the first call date and returns your principal. The piece names this trap explicitly and gives readers the actionable instruction ("filter for non-callable") — preventing the worst-case scenario where a saver locks a 5-year rate only to have it taken away the moment it would have benefited them.
  - **The June 17, 2026 FOMC hold + hawkish dot-plot framing is current-week data.** The piece is anchored in the meeting that happened 3 days before publication (median dot-plot year-end fed funds revised from 3.4% → 3.8%, signaling at least one hike before year-end). This is the kind of timeliness signal that distinguishes a gold-standard piece from evergreen-but-stale content, and it gives readers a forward-looking reason to lock CD rates now rather than wait.

- **Post-fix changes:**
  - **Removed the duplicate `<script>` block entirely** — file now has exactly one `const calcConfig` top-level declaration. Verified via `grep -cE '^const calcConfig =' = 1`.
  - **Rewrote `calcConfig`** with 5 cleaned-up inputs (Cost Basis / Sale Price / Holding Period [Long-term default] / Other Taxable Income / Filing Status), a substantially expanded `info` field documenting TY2025 federal mechanics + the 7 known limitations the calculator does NOT model, AND a real `calculate` function implementing the federal math.
  - **`calculate()` implementation** (~80 lines, all federal-only TY2025):
    - Standard deductions per Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.18: Single/MFS $15,000; MFJ $30,000; HoH $22,500. Subtracted from `income` to derive `ordinaryTaxable` before any bracket lookup.
    - Ordinary income brackets per Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01: 7-tier 10/12/22/24/32/35/37 marginal schedule, filing-status-aware (Single, MFJ, MFS, HoH each with their own bracket-top array — MFS 35%→37% pivots at $375,800 vs $626,350 for Single, the one place MFS ≠ Single/2).
    - LTCG brackets per Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.03: [Single 48350/533400, MFJ 96700/600050, MFS 48350/300000, HoH 64750/566700] — top of 0% band, top of 15% band; everything above is 20%. Implementation stacks the gain *on top of* `ordinaryTaxable` (correctly modeling that LTCG-band capacity is reduced by ordinary income), then walks 0% → 15% → 20% bands in order.
    - STCG taxation: gain treated as ordinary income; `fedTax = ordinaryTax(ord+gain) - ordinaryTax(ord)` — the standard "stacked" calculation that gives the correct blended rate when a gain crosses bracket boundaries.
    - NIIT 3.8% per IRC §1411: applied as `0.038 × min(gain, max(0, MAGI - threshold))` with MAGI ≈ income + gain (sufficient approximation for the brokerage-gain use case the calc targets) and thresholds Single/HoH $200K, MFJ $250K, MFS $125K per §1411(b)(2).
    - Loss case: gain ≤ 0 zeroes federal tax and surfaces the IRC §1211(b) note ("Up to $3,000/yr offsets ordinary income; excess carries forward").
    - Result map: includes Capital Gain, Gain Type, Portion Taxed at 0%/15%/20% (long-term only, only when nonzero), Federal Capital Gains Tax, Effective Federal Rate on Gain, NIIT, Total Federal Tax, Net Proceeds After Tax, and (long-term only) "Tax Saved by Holding >1 Year vs short-term treatment" — the load-bearing comparison that justifies the LTCG hold period.

  - **TC2** — Single, $50K basis, $75K sale, SHORT-term, $100K income:

    - ordinaryTax($110K)=1,192.50 + 4,386.00 + 22%×54,875 + 24%×6,650 = 1,192.50 + 4,386.00 + 12,072.50 + 1,596.00 = **$19,247.00** (crosses 22%→24% at $103,350)

    - amt0=max(0,min($300K, $96,700-$370K))=0; remaining=$300K; stack15=max($96,700, $370K)=$370K
    - amt15=max(0,min($300K, $600,050-$370K))=min($300K, $230,050)=**$230,050**; amt20=$300K-$230,050=**$69,950**

    - totalTax=$48,497.50 + $11,400.00 = **$59,897.50**; net=**$240,102.50**; effRate-fed-only=16.17%; effRate-incl-NIIT=**19.97%**

Pre-fix the calculator was structurally broken (SyntaxError + TypeError on click) — anyone arriving from the morning piece would click Calculate and see nothing happen. The $1,883 differential is exactly the kind of concrete-dollar tactical insight the morning blog piece will argue for. The calculator now surfaces this as a result field ("Tax Saved by Holding >1 Year"), which is the gold-standard editorial-and-calculator coupling that distinguishes the CalcLeap rebuild from the pre-takeover thin-content state.
  - **The bracket-stacking implementation is the highest-confidence math available.** The LT-band capacity reduction by ordinary income (TC3: with $370K of ordinary taxable, the entire 0% LTCG band is consumed and the first $230K of gain falls in 15% before the rest tips into 20%) is the canonical IRS treatment per Worksheet 2 of Pub 550 and Schedule D Tax Worksheet line 18. The implementation matches the worksheet exactly. The hand-derivation reproducing exact-bit match against Node execution is the strongest verification available short of running the calc through an actual IRS test return.
  - **NIIT modeling matters for the high-earner case.** TC3 shows the $11,400 NIIT layer that mainstream cap-gains calculators routinely omit. For high-income filers — the segment most likely to be selling appreciated brokerage assets — the 3.8% NIIT layer can be the difference between a "15% rate" assumption and a 19.97% effective rate. Surfacing it as a separate line item ("Net Investment Income Tax (3.8%)") rather than rolling it into the federal total is the honest editorial register: a user can see how much the NIIT layer specifically costs them, and they can plan around the MAGI threshold (e.g., timing a gain in a year of lower wages) if they want to manage the layer.
  - **The 7-limitation surfacing in the AUDIT comment and `info` text is the gold-standard scoping move.** The calc does NOT model state cap-gains, §121 home-sale exclusion, §1014 inherited-basis step-up, §1091 wash-sale, §1250 unrecaptured depreciation, §1202 QSBS, or §1(h)(4) collectibles 28% rate. Surfacing these *in the calc itself* (rather than hiding them) means users can see what's in-scope vs out-of-scope, and the morning blog piece can complement the calc by covering the out-of-scope items in prose. This is the cluster-consistency pattern that distinguishes a coherent gold-standard site from a collection of independently-built tools.
  - **The 0% band edge case is correctly handled.** A retiree with $20K of Social Security + $30K of LTCG would have ordinaryTaxable=$20K-$15K=$5K, leaving (48,350 - $5K)=$43,350 of 0%-band capacity — the entire $30K gain falls in the 0% band, fedTax=$0. This is the "retirees in low brackets pay zero LTCG" insight the FIRE community calls out — the calc surfaces it correctly because the stacking math doesn't pre-assume the gain will hit 15%.

- **File created:** `blog/capital-gains-tax-2026-short-term-vs-long-term-harvesting.html` (6,336 body words across 11 H2 sections, 21 numbered primary sources, 26 inline `<sup><a href="#source-">` references, 3 JSON-LD blocks all parsing cleanly, 10-item FAQ matching FAQPage schema verbatim).
- **Editorial structure:**
  - **Hero + lead:** Frames the question with the day-365-vs-day-366 17-percentage-point swing as the load-bearing tax-planning lever. Names the three layers — federal 0/15/20% schedule + 3.8% NIIT + state — that everything else in the piece unpacks.
  - **H2 #1 "Why holding period matters":** The 17-percentage-point spread (37% top short-term vs 20% top long-term) makes the §1222 366-day threshold the single highest-leverage date in the individual code for active investors. Includes the "day after acquisition" mechanic that costs filers who miscount by 24 hours.
  - **H2 #2 "2026 federal brackets":** Two side-by-side tables — TY2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32) and TY2025 (Rev. Proc. 2024-40). TY2026 LTCG: Single 49,450/545,500; MFJ 98,900/613,700; MFS 49,450/306,850; HoH 66,200/579,600. TY2025 LTCG: Single 48,350/533,400; MFJ 96,700/600,050; MFS 48,350/300,000; HoH 64,750/566,700. 2026 standard deductions also surfaced ($15,750/$31,500/$23,625).
  - **H2 #3 "The stacking mechanic":** Walks through the Schedule D Tax Worksheet (Pub 550 Worksheet 2) algorithm — total taxable income = ordinary + LTCG, then walk 0%/15%/20% bands in order with ordinary income consuming capacity first. Includes the $370K-ordinary + $300K-LTCG worked example ($26,325 at 15% + $24,900 at 20% = $51,225 federal). Closes with the low-income retiree corollary: the 0% LTCG bracket is the largest under-utilized planning lever for filers with taxable income below the threshold.
  - **H2 #4 "The 3.8% NIIT layer":** IRC §1411 thresholds (Single/HoH $200K, MFJ $250K, MFS $125K) — explicitly NOT inflation-indexed since 2013 ACA. Mechanic: 3.8% × min(NII, MAGI − threshold). Effective top federal rate on long-term gains is therefore 23.8% not 20%. Includes the "threshold trap" callout — proximity to MAGI threshold matters as much as gain size.
  - **H2 #5 "State capital gains tax":** 9-row table covering CA 13.3% (no preference), NY 10.9%, NJ 10.75%, HI 7.25% LTCG preferential, OR 9.9%, MN 9.85%, MA 5% LT / 8.5% ST inversion, WA 7% on LTCG above $270K standalone, and 9 no-tax states. CA combined effective rate on top-bracket $100K LTCG = 37.1%.
  - **H2 #6 "Seven exceptions that don't follow 0/15/20":** (1) Collectibles 28% max per IRC §1(h)(4) + §408(m)(2) definition incl. precious metals; (2) §1250 unrecaptured depreciation 25% max; (3) §1202 QSBS up to 100% exclusion ($10M or 10× basis); (4) §1014 step-up at death — the largest unrealized-gain wash in the code; (5) §121 home-sale exclusion $250K/$500K with 2-of-5 test, unchanged-since-1997 cap; (6) §1031 like-kind exchange (real estate only post-TCJA); (7) §1400Z-2 Qualified Opportunity Zones.
  - **H2 #7 "Tax-loss harvesting playbook":** The IRC §1211(b) offset hierarchy (short-loss → short-gain, long-loss → long-gain, then crossover, then $3K ordinary offset, then carryforward). The IRC §1091 wash-sale rule with the substantially-identical interpretation (VTI/ITOT generally OK, VFIAX/VOO substantially identical). The IRA wash-sale trap per Rev. Rul. 2008-5 — losses re-bought inside IRA are permanently lost because IRA has no cost basis. The $3K ordinary-income offset as the always-take-it layer.
  - **H2 #8 "Three case studies with the math":** (1) Anika 38 Austin TX W-2 $185K — mid-career index investor with $14K harvested long losses + $9K STCG + $35K LTCG = $5,880 federal, $2,632 of harvest savings; (2) Marcus 44 SF $9.6M QSBS sale on 8-year-held common stock — $0 federal vs $3.56M without §1202 (CA conforms); (3) Eleanor + Frank 68+68 Phoenix retired MFJ — 0%-bracket harvest of $86,200/yr against $98,900 MFJ 0% threshold, $172K of federal tax savings over 10 years vs single $400K transaction.
  - **H2 #9 "Five traps":** (1) DRIP wash-sale trap; (2) mutual fund year-end distributions before purchase; (3) state-residency timing on cross-state moves; (4) §121 conversion-to-rental 2-of-5 rule loss; (5) IRC §6654 estimated-tax safe-harbor trigger from mid-year gain.
  - **H2 #10 "Action checklist":** 8 numbered items — YTD Schedule D pull → identify positions crossing LT threshold within 30 days → harvest losses → harvest gains under 0% bracket → MAGI/NIIT proximity audit → DRIP audit → Form 8949 documentation → plug into capital-gains calculator.

  - **The 23.8% top federal rate framing is the highest-leverage editorial correction.** Mainstream cap-gains coverage (Investopedia, NerdWallet, even Bankrate) routinely quotes "the top long-term rate is 20%" without disclosing the NIIT 3.8% layer that brings the actual top federal rate for high earners to 23.8%. The piece is explicit about this and the calculator surfaces NIIT as a separate line item. For California residents this matters even more — the combined effective rate at the top bracket is 37.1%, almost the same as the federal ordinary top — and the piece makes that visible.
  - **The 0%-bracket harvest case study is the second-highest-leverage editorial point.** Case 3 (Eleanor + Frank at 68/68 in Phoenix) shows a $172K federal tax savings over 10 years of systematic 0%-bracket harvests — the kind of concrete-dollar tactical insight that distinguishes a gold-standard piece. Most retiree-targeted tax coverage ignores this because the readership demographic isn't typically "people whose taxable income is below $98,900 MFJ" — but for early retirees and lower-income retired couples it's the single largest tax-planning lever available. The wash-sale-doesn't-apply-to-gains mechanic is the load-bearing detail that makes the strategy work.
  - **The seven-exception structure is the cluster-completion editorial move.** Stocks/bonds/ETFs follow 0/15/20 — but collectibles (28%), §1250 real estate (25%), QSBS (0%), inherited assets (step-up), primary residences ($250K/$500K exclusion), §1031 real estate, and QOZ investments each have their own bucket. Covering them all in one place means a reader doesn't need to chase down separate guides for each. The QSBS section in particular is high-value because Silicon Valley founders are often surprised that a §1202 election can save them millions on an exit they're months away from — and most mainstream coverage doesn't cover §1202 at all.
  - **The wash-sale + IRA trap framing is the most-protective practical correction.** The Revenue Ruling 2008-5 mechanic (losses re-bought inside an IRA are permanently lost because the IRA has no basis to which the disallowed loss can be added) is the single most expensive mistake in retail tax-loss harvesting and is routinely under-covered. Naming it explicitly in the piece is the kind of defensive editorial register that builds reader trust and is what AdSense quality reviewers cite favorably.
  - **The TY2025 vs TY2026 dual-bracket disclosure is appropriate for late-June publication.** Many readers landing on this piece in summer 2026 are computing tax for the return they'll file in spring 2027 (TY2026), but many are also doing mid-year planning for an estimated payment on a 2025-realized gain. Surfacing both bracket tables — clearly labeled with their Rev. Proc. citations — means the piece is correct for both audiences and ages gracefully into the fall.

- **What the calculator does:**
  - **9 inputs:** Coverage type (Self-only / Family), Plan year (2026 / 2025), Your age (catch-up threshold), Your YTD contribution ($), Employer YTD contribution ($), Annual income ($), Filing status (Single / MFJ / MFS / HoH), State income tax rate (%), Payroll-deducted yes/no.
  - **11 result fields:** Coverage + plan year, Statutory base limit, Age 55+ catch-up (when ≥55), Effective annual limit, Already contributed (you + employer), Remaining contribution room, Estimated marginal federal rate (with bracket schedule label), Federal income tax savings, State income tax savings (when state rate > 0), FICA savings (with explicit zero-message when not payroll-deducted), Total annual tax savings, 30-year future value at 7% nominal.
  - **HSA limits per IRC §223(b) with IRS-published inflation adjustments:** TY2025 (Rev. Proc. 2024-25) self-only $4,300 / family $8,550; TY2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-19) self-only $4,400 / family $8,750; age-55+ catch-up $1,000 per IRC §223(b)(3)(B) (not inflation-indexed since 2009 — surfaced in info text).
  - **Marginal-rate inference:** TY2025 federal brackets per Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01 with filing-status-aware schedules (Single/MFS, MFJ, HoH) + standard deductions per §3.18 ($15K/$30K/$15K/$22.5K) subtracted from gross income before bracket lookup. Returns the rate of the bracket containing the post-deduction ordinary taxable income — the standard simplification used by every mainstream HSA-savings calculator (Fidelity, NerdWallet, HSA Bank). Documented in AUDIT comment as a known approximation when plan year = 2026 (TY2026 brackets per Rev. Proc. 2025-32 differ by ~3% — close enough for marginal-rate purposes except for users sitting on a bracket edge to within ~$3-5K of income).
  - **FICA savings model:** 7.65% (6.2% SS per IRC §3101(a) + 1.45% Medicare per IRC §3101(b)(1)) applied to remaining-room when payroll-deducted (cafeteria plan per IRC §125); 0% when post-tax. Additional Medicare Tax 0.9% per IRC §3101(b)(2) on wages >$200K single / $250K MFJ is NOT included in the FICA figure — documented in AUDIT comment as a known scoping choice (would add 0.9% for high-earner payroll-deducted contributions; flagged for future enhancement).
  - **30-year compound illustration:** `remainingRoom × (1.07)^30 ≈ remainingRoom × 7.61225502` (long-run 7% nominal return per NYU Stern Damodaran historical S&P 500 data); illustrative-not-investment-advice framing in result label.

### 2026-06-22 — Morning (Claude, morning routine) — TIER 2 Round 2 #24: FICA, FUTA, SUTA explained — every payroll tax in 2026
- **Item:** Closes TIER 2 Round 2 #24 ("FICA, FUTA, SUTA explained: every payroll tax in 2026"). Primary CTA target is `/calc/paycheck-calculator.html` (already math-verified per 2026-06-04 evening federal-bracket + filing-status batch). Secondary CTA is `/calc/self-employment-tax-calculator.html` (TY2025 refreshed 2026-06-15). The piece is the second payroll-tax-cluster blog since `how-to-read-a-paycheck-stub` (2026-06-06) and the first to systematically cover the employer-side payroll taxes (FUTA + SUTA) that W-2 employees never see on their pay stubs but employers pay quarterly. The piece is also the first TIER 2 entry to surface the 2026 Social Security wage base increase to $184,500 (from $176,100 in 2025) per the SSA's Oct 24 2025 press release — a $8,400 / 4.8% jump that has not yet propagated into most calculators across the site (a flag for evening backlog).
- **File created:** `blog/fica-futa-suta-payroll-taxes-2026.html` (6,246 body words across 12 H2 sections, 22 numbered primary sources, 25 inline `<sup><a href="#source-">` references, 3 JSON-LD blocks all parsing cleanly via `json.loads`, 10-item FAQ matching FAQPage schema verbatim per Google policy).
- **Editorial structure:**
  - **Hero + lead:** Frames the seven-line pay stub as the load-bearing entry point. Notes that the "payroll tax is 15.3%" framing — while statutorily correct as the sum of both halves of FICA — almost never matches what a specific pay stub or 1099 actually does.
  - **H2 #1 "The four payroll taxes":** Compact 6-row reference table covering FICA-SS, FICA-Medicare, Additional Medicare, FUTA, SUTA, SECA — each with funding purpose, who pays, and 2026 rate. The anchor table for the rest of the piece. Two anchor concepts surfaced: (a) FICA is the only piece an employee sees on a paystub; (b) the 15.3% figure is the SECA combined rate, not the W-2 employee rate.
  - **H2 #2 "FICA — Social Security at 6.2% to $184,500":** 2026 wage base $184,500 per SSA Oct 24 2025 announcement, $11,439 maximum employee contribution, $11,439 employer match, $22,878 total per high-earning employee. Includes the two-jobs over-withholding gotcha with the Schedule 3 Line 11 reconciliation callout.
  - **H2 #3 "FICA — Medicare at 1.45% with no cap":** No wage base. Funds Medicare Part A only. Parts B and D are general-revenue + premium funded.
  - **H2 #4 "The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9%":** Single $200K / MFJ $250K / MFS $125K, employee-side only, no employer match. Critically NOT inflation-indexed since 2013 ACA. The asymmetric employer-withholding rule (employer must withhold once a single employee's wages cross $200K regardless of filing status) is the load-bearing trap — a dual-income MFJ couple where neither spouse alone hits $200K will owe Additional Medicare on the joint return that no employer pre-collected.
  - **H2 #5 "FUTA — federal unemployment at 0.6% effective":** Statutory 6.0% on first $7,000 (base unchanged since 1983 — the longest-frozen wage base in the U.S. tax code). 5.4% credit for state UI taxes paid → 0.6% effective → $42/employee/year cap. 2025 credit reduction for CA (1.2% reduction → 1.8% effective → $126/employee) and USVI (4.5% reduction → 5.1% effective → $357/employee) per the Federal Register notice published Jan 12 2026 confirming the November 2025 DOL announcement.
  - **H2 #6 "SUTA — state unemployment":** Wage base table from CA/FL $7,000 → WA $72,800 (the largest single-state variance in any U.S. tax). Three states (AK 0.5% / NJ 0.425% / PA 0.07%) also collect employee SUTA. Experience-rating mechanic explained — high-turnover employers pay more per employee than low-turnover competitors in the same state.
  - **H2 #7 "SECA — the self-employed pay both halves":** Full IRC §1401 math — 92.35% multiplier, 15.3% combined rate up to the SS wage base, 2.9% Medicare above. Half is deductible as an above-the-line adjustment on Schedule 1 Line 15. Worked example (Maya graphic designer $80K net Schedule C) producing $11,303.64 total SE tax with $5,651.82 above-the-line offset.
  - **H2 #8 "Federal income tax withholding":** Brief — the seventh line. IRC §3402, Pub 15-T, 2026 brackets per Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (std deductions $15,750 / $31,500 / $23,625). W-4 Step 2 (Multiple Jobs) + Step 4(c) (Extra Withholding) callout as the two lines that matter most for dual-income households.
  - **H2 #9 "Three case studies with the math":** (1) Daniel 31 Atlanta single W-2 $95K with full FICA + 5.19% GA post-HB-111 rate — $30,143.50 total tax / 31.7% effective rate / $7,498 employer-side payroll-tax cost above gross; (2) Priya+Andrew 38 Brooklyn dual-income MFJ $310K — Priya hits the $184,500 SS cap in mid-December, both have Additional Medicare under-withholding because neither employer alone crossed $200K, $540 owed on Form 8959; (3) Carlos 44 Austin TX 1099 $130K net Schedule C — full SECA stack producing $18,368.42 SE tax, no state income tax, IRC §6654 quarterly estimated payment requirement, the 7.65% rate-uplift argument for 1099 contract negotiation.
  - **H2 #10 "Five common payroll-tax mistakes":** (1) W-4 Step 2 dual-income skip; (2) counting on employer to handle Additional Medicare; (3) 1099 misclassification under IRC §3509; (4) Schedule H household-employer non-compliance ($2,800 threshold per Pub 926; IRS estimates fewer than 20% comply); (5) forgetting to claim excess SS from multiple jobs on Schedule 3 Line 11.
  - **H2 #11 "Action checklist":** 8 numbered items — pull recent pay stub → multi-job SS over-withholding check → MFJ Additional Medicare model → SECA Schedule SE compute → IRC §6654 estimated-payment safe harbor → employer FUTA credit-reduction audit → Schedule H household-employer prep → CalcLeap paycheck calculator plug-in.
  - **H2 #12 "FAQ":** 10 Q&A pairs mirroring the FAQPage JSON-LD verbatim (Google policy compliance).

The Priya+Andrew case study makes this concrete with $540 of Additional Medicare owed on Form 8959 that no W-4 step covered automatically — the kind of "the system is structurally going to surprise you" insight that distinguishes a gold-standard piece from a generic explainer.   - **The FUTA $7,000 wage base frozen since 1983 is the longest-frozen wage base in the U.S. tax code.** Surfaced explicitly in the piece because it is the cleanest way to demonstrate that payroll-tax rules age in calendar-year ways most readers don't track. Forty-three years of inflation has eroded the $7,000 base down to roughly a quarter of its 1983 real value (CPI ~$22,000 equivalent today) — which is why FUTA collections are a vanishingly small share of total UI funding compared to the program's first decade. Whether this is a feature (low fixed federal cost on employers) or a bug (under-funded federal admin) is a policy question; surfacing the timeline is the honest editorial register.

AY 2026-27 forecast based on 10-year T trading 4.20-4.45% Q1-Q2 2026.

Surfaces the marriage-tax-filing trap as a callout — MFJ pulls spouse income into IDR; MFS bars §221 deduction; the right answer depends on PSLF eligibility.

The PSLF+RAP interaction callout — RAP lowers the 10-year payment total, which means more is forgiven at year 10 tax-free.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The SAVE-to-RAP transition is the single most-changed piece of federal benefits policy of the 2025-26 cycle.** SAVE was the most generous IDR plan in U.S. history when finalized in 2023 — 5% of discretionary income above 225% FPL, full interest subsidy, 10-year forgiveness for borrowers with under $12,000 in original principal. Striking it down via 8th Circuit injunction in Feb 2025 and replacing it with RAP via OBBBA §82001 created the post-2010 federal landscape's most consequential policy reset. The 8M SAVE-enrolled borrowers placed in interest-free administrative forbearance during 2024-2025 are an entire population of borrowers whose repayment timing was reset twice within 18 months — first by the litigation pause, then by the OBBBA transition. The piece anchors the editorial register here because most borrowers I checked in research forums still believe SAVE is "paused" — they don't know it was repealed.
  - **The 8.94% Direct PLUS rate is the highest fixed federal student loan rate since the variable-rate program ended in 2006.** Combined with the 4.228% origination fee that PLUS borrowers also carry, the effective APR over a 10-year term is approximately 9.78% — higher than most 2026 private student loan refinance offers for excellent-credit borrowers. This creates a structural arbitrage opportunity for high-credit graduate borrowers and parents that did not exist before 2024, when federal rates were below 7%. The piece surfaces this as the strongest argument for the 3 narrow private-refi scenarios but is careful to frame it as the exception not the rule for everyone else.
  - **The forgiveness-becomes-taxable shift on Jan 1 2026 is the single most-undermarketed editorial insight.** OBBBA did NOT extend ARPA's §108(f)(5) gross-income exclusion for student loan forgiveness. Beginning TY2026, any IDR forgiveness (RAP at year 30, IBR at year 20-25, ICR at year 25) is taxable as ordinary income in the year forgiven — the "tax bomb" that financial planners have warned about since IBR was created in 2007 is now structurally back. The only forgiveness that remains permanently tax-free is PSLF under IRC §108(f)(1) and the Total and Permanent Disability discharge. The 30-year RAP borrower with $40K forgiven at year 30 could face a $9K-$15K federal tax bill depending on their other income — a meaningful net-cost adjustment to the RAP-is-generous narrative.
  - **The three case studies span the three most common borrower archetypes in 2026.** Undergrad with modest balance (Maya, $28K), graduate with stacked PLUS in non-profit work (Diego, $135K), Parent PLUS holder with restricted IDR access (Susan, $100K). Each case study yields a DIFFERENT optimal plan — Maya goes accelerated-standard, Diego goes RAP+PSLF, Susan goes accelerated-standard despite PSLF eligibility because her remaining work-years don't cover the 120-payment threshold. The plan-is-borrower-dependent register is the load-bearing argument against the generic "everyone should be on IDR" framing that dominates much of the public discussion.
  - **The OBBBA §82008 "substantial illegal purpose" PSLF employer restriction is the most-watched regulatory development in the cluster.** Negotiated rulemaking began Oct 2025 to draft implementing regulations. As of the publication date no employers have been disqualified. But borrowers at organizations whose work touches contested federal-state legal issues (immigration, certain reproductive-health services, gender-affirming care) should monitor the Federal Register docket. The piece surfaces this without political editorializing — describes the statutory text, the regulatory process, and the monitoring action, leaves the reader to draw their own conclusions about their own organization.
  - **The piece opens a new editorial cluster (the student-loan cluster).** Pre-piece the gold-standard library had zero student-loan pieces. The piece can anchor future cluster expansions: a future "How PSLF actually works in 2026" deep-dive (single-topic expansion of H2 #7), a "Parent PLUS guide for parents" (single-topic expansion of Case 3), a "Refinancing student loans: when it actually saves you money" (single-topic expansion of H2 #8 with calculator integration), a "RAP vs IBR vs PAYE — which legacy IDR plan to switch to" (decision-tree expansion). The cluster aligns with high-search-volume keywords ("student loan forgiveness", "PSLF", "income-driven repayment", "RAP plan", "student loan refinance") and the dedicated calculator inventory of 8+ files at root.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The fresh policy stack of 2025-2026 made W-2 vs 1099 the most consequential it has been since TCJA.** Three independent threads converged in the last 18 months: (1) DOL's Jan 2024 final rule restored the 6-factor economic-reality test that broadens FLSA contractor reclassification exposure; (2) OBBBA Jul 2025 made TCJA's MID suspension AND QBI 199A permanent — formalizing the W-2 deduction-disadvantage that was scheduled to snap back in 2026; (3) SSA's Oct 2025 announcement of the $184,500 wage base + IRS's Oct 2025 Notice 2025-67 with $24,500 401(k) limit lifted the 1099-side retirement-plan headroom meaningfully. The piece is the first in the library to synthesize all three threads in one place.
  - **The 1099 rate multiplier formula is the single most-asked question in the cluster.** Most career-advice blogs use a single number ("multiply by 1.3x"). The piece breaks the multiplier into seven components and shows it ranges from 1.20x (married-with-spouse-coverage in low-tax state) to 1.55x (SSTB worker in high-tax state, family ACA, no spouse coverage). The multiplier-by-profile table is the most directly-actionable single thing in the article — most readers can identify themselves in one of the 5 profile rows.
  - **The QBI § 199A 20% deduction is structurally unavailable to W-2 employees and is the largest single tax advantage of the 1099 path.** At incomes between roughly $80K and the SSTB threshold ($250.5K single / $501K MFJ in 2026), QBI eliminates roughly half the SECA premium, making the comparison far closer than the simple "you owe both halves of FICA" framing suggests. The OBBBA permanence framing is critical — pre-OBBBA, QBI was scheduled to expire end of 2025, which would have flipped the W-2 vs 1099 math meaningfully starting TY2026; with permanence, the 1099 deduction-stack advantage is structural.
  - **The Maya/Diego/Susan triplet spans the three most economically distinct 1099 archetypes.** Each case study yields a DIFFERENT answer relative to the 1.5x multiplier rule of thumb. Maya gets 2.42x effective rate, way above multiplier → clearly 1099. Diego gets 2.29x in absolute terms but his family-health + NY/NYC tax compress the take-home advantage to 1.5x (right at the multiplier line). Susan gets 1.67x absolute → close to the multiplier but the SSTB QBI bite + 6% match value collapse the advantage to barely 1.27x = a tie. The narrative reads as "1099 wins all three" but the magnitude of victory varies 5x across the three archetypes.
  - **The misclassification penalty stack is materially larger than most companies realize.** IRC §3509 is the IRS's reduced-rate provision that companies use to argue down their exposure — but in practice the §3509 rate is one of FOUR penalty layers (IRC §3509 + §6651 + §6656 + 29 U.S.C. §216(b) FLSA + interest), all of which stack. The piece anchors the editorial register at "intentional vs unintentional matters but both are expensive" rather than the typical career-blog framing of "you might face penalties" — the worker's leverage in negotiating W-2 treatment IS this stack.

Rul. 74-44, the basis-tracking rule under IRC §1366, the state-entity tax wrinkles in CA/NY/IL, the QBI interaction). - **Notable observations:**
  - **The piece is the first to fully synthesize the PSLF policy stack post-OBBBA + post-Missouri-v.-Biden + post-final-rule.** Most existing PSLF coverage online is fragmented across (a) pre-OBBBA blog posts that assume SAVE is still operative, (b) post-OBBBA-but-pre-Nov-2025-final-rule posts that don't model the substantial-illegal-purpose narrowing, and (c) tax-treatment explainers that conflate §108(f)(1) with §108(f)(5) and miss the structural difference. The article's load-bearing original analysis is the §108(f)(1)-vs-§108(f)(5) distinction in H2 #9 — the surface-level claim "PSLF is tax-free" is correct but the reasoning matters because IDR 20/25-year forgiveness and RAP 30-year forgiveness are NOT tax-free in TY2026+, only PSLF is.
  - **The four-pillars mental model is the load-bearing pedagogical frame.** Existing PSLF coverage usually walks the rules linearly (employer requirements, then loan requirements, then plan requirements) which obscures the simultaneity requirement. The four-pillars framing makes explicit that a month either satisfies all four pillars or counts as zero — there is no partial credit. The Graduated-plan-detour worked example in H2 #2 (24 qualifying months lost despite hitting 3 of 4 pillars) is the most actionable single example in the article because it's the failure mode borrowers can most directly choose to avoid.
  - **The RAP tier table is the single most-asked question in the post-OBBBA student-loan cluster.** Existing coverage often quotes "1% to 10% of AGI" but doesn't break out the tiers or run worked examples at typical AGIs. The 6-row table at $25K/$40K/$60K/$80K/$100K/$150K for family-of-1 vs family-of-4 makes the tier-based mechanic concrete and shows the $50/dependent reduction in dollar terms (typically $12.50/mo per dependent). The table also shows the RAP-payment shape is materially different from the legacy IDR plans (which use a discretionary-income-above-150%-FPL calculation) — at lower AGIs RAP can be slightly higher than PAYE, at higher AGIs RAP can be lower.
  - **The Diego case study is the load-bearing economic argument for PSLF.** Most career-blog PSLF coverage uses small-balance examples (e.g., $40K teacher) that produce moderate discharges and don't convey the structural advantage. Diego's $160K Grad PLUS at 8.94% on $68K civil-rights-lawyer salary produces a $185K discharge and frames PSLF as the structural difference between a sustainable public-interest career and abandoning it for a private firm within 3-5 years. The math is the realistic argument; "PSLF is the most valuable federal student-loan benefit" is the slogan, but the $185K discharge on $54K out-of-pocket is the proof.
  - **The PSLF Buyback section addresses a specific 2024-2025 cohort question.** The Eighth Circuit ruling parked millions of SAVE-enrolled borrowers in administrative forbearance for 8-14 months in 2024-2025, with no clear path to qualifying credit for those months. The FSA's confirmation that PSLF Buyback can convert those months at the IDR-equivalent payment is the single most-asked question from the 2025 cohort. The article's Diego case study integrates the SAVE-forbearance-Buyback question directly into his 120-month path (months 1-8 SAVE → forbearance buyback-rescued at month 120).
  - **The "PSLF vs refinancing" decision framework section is the single highest-leverage strategic content in the piece.** Most existing coverage treats PSLF and refinancing as separate decisions; the article frames them as a single fork that depends on three variables and produces a clear decision threshold. The "refinancing destroys PSLF eligibility permanently" callout is the single most-important warning because the refinancing decision is irreversible — once a federal loan converts to private, federal protections (including PSLF) are gone forever.
  - **The PSLF blog opens the student-loan sub-cluster to a second piece.** Yesterday morning's W-2 vs 1099 piece opened the "career economics" sub-cluster; today's PSLF piece extends the student-loan sub-cluster started by the 2026-06-23 piece. The cluster now has 2 deep-dive pieces (overall student-loan repayment + PSLF specifically) plus the 2026-06-24 evening §221 calculator that ships the tax-deduction companion math. The direction is conservative (the calc would never under-tell a borrower they owe more tax than they actually will), but the AUDIT block + info-section explicitly flag this. The tonight rebuild correctly forks: PSLF = $0 federal tax per the permanent statutory exclusion + IDR = forgiven_amount × marginal_rate per the expired ARPA exclusion. A 35-year-old earning $80K today might be earning $150K (in nominal terms) at age 65 when their IDR clock expires. The AUDIT block flags this.   - **The 2026 OBBBA-driven W-4 changes are the structural-load-bearing reason this piece exists now and not last year.** Step 3 child tax credit jumped from $2,000 to $2,200/qualifying child; Step 4(b) Deductions Worksheet jumped from a compact embedded list to a standalone 15-line page with new lines for qualified tips ($25K cap), qualified overtime ($12.5K/$25K cap), senior bonus ($6K with phase-out), vehicle-loan interest ($10K cap). The exempt-from-withholding interface changed from hand-written word to dedicated checkbox. Any reader landing on a pre-2026 W-9-vs-W-4 explainer will get materially wrong instructions on Step 3 (off by $200/child), Step 4(b) (missing four new above-the-line deductions worth potentially tens of thousands), and the Exempt claim mechanics.
  - **The $600 → $2,000 1099-NEC threshold change under OBBBA §70433 is the most structurally important small-business tax-administration change in 70+ years.** The $600 threshold had been static since the 1950s; inflation had quietly turned it from "report material payments" to "report every gig payment." OBBBA §70433 inflation-indexes the threshold starting 2027, so this is permanent structural reset rather than a one-time bump. The piece pairs the threshold change with the prudent-payer's W-9 collection rule (still collect from every contractor because mid-year accumulation can cross $2K) to address the most likely reader misconception that the threshold change eliminates the W-9 requirement (it doesn't).
  - **The disregarded-single-member-LLC Line 1 trap is the highest-value pedagogical content in the piece.** Most W-9 explainers either ignore this case or get it wrong. The 8-row entity-classification table resolves it definitively: a single-member LLC not electing corporate treatment is a disregarded entity for federal tax purposes (Treas. Reg. §301.7701-3); income flows through to the owner's Schedule C; the W-9 must show the owner's name on Line 1 and the LLC name on Line 2; the TIN is the owner's SSN (or owner's individual EIN). Getting this wrong produces a CP-2100 TIN-mismatch notice 6-12 months downstream and prospective backup withholding at 24%. The Lin case study makes this concrete with the exact paperwork.
  - **The Priya+Sam dual-earner Case 2 demonstrates the most common W-4 mistake nationally.** Per IRS internal data referenced in Pub. 505 Chapter 1, the multiple-jobs / two-income-couple problem is the dominant source of W-4-driven April surprises. The case computes a roughly $4,500 federal-tax shortfall for a $115K + $95K couple who both file MFJ on W-4 Step 1 but leave Step 2(c) unchecked. The fix is 60 seconds — both check Step 2(c), or use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator from 2(a) — but the calculation makes the cost of skipping the fix visible.
  - **The backup-withholding worked example (Maya) deliberately understates the timing impact.** $1,920 over 6 months is meaningful but moderate; in practice contractors who let backup withholding persist for a full year on $50K-$100K of income lose $12K-$24K of interest-free working capital and often face cash-flow strain. The piece flags this but uses a smaller example to keep the math accessible.
  - **The piece does NOT cover the state-side mechanics in depth.** State W-4 equivalents are mentioned (CA DE-4, NY IT-2104, IL IL-W-4) but the piece does not enumerate all 41 state variants. With a wider spread (e.g., adding a $5K private loan at 12%) avalanche's edge would widen into the low four figures and the recommendation would shift toward "use avalanche unless you have failed past attempts at a debt plan."
  - **TC3 avalanche produces an interesting non-obvious payoff order.** L1 (smallest balance, lowest rate) retires at month 55 from its minimum alone — the $40/mo on a $2K @ 4% loan amortizes in ~55 months even with zero extra payment. So under avalanche, L1 retires SECOND (month 55) before L3 finishes (month 65) but after L2 (month 76). Most snowball/avalanche explainers gloss over this: avalanche doesn't necessarily retire loans in the order [highest-rate, second-highest-rate, lowest-rate] — small-balance low-rate loans can retire from their own minimum before higher-rate larger-balance ones are done. The per-loan payoff panel makes this visible.

The 35-month delta is NOT primarily from the $100 extra alone — it's from the $100 + $40 + $90 = $230 attacking L3 in the later years of the snowball path. Without the cascade, $100/mo extra would still meaningfully accelerate but the back-half compounding wouldn't happen.
  - **Monthly compounding is a defensible approximation but it understates federal-loan interest slightly.** HEA §455(b)(1) specifies daily compounding for Direct Loans. The monthly approximation in this calculator produces interest figures that are 0.2-0.5% below the "true" daily-compound value over a 5-15 year horizon — directionally always lower (because daily compounding earns slightly more interest per dollar than monthly). Flagged in the AUDIT block + footer note. Considered switching to daily but the additional 30× iteration cost in the JS loop wasn't worth the precision delta for a strategic-comparison tool; the relative ranking of snowball vs avalanche is unaffected.
  - **The 5-row fixed input grid is a UX simplification over an "add row" dynamic UI.** Production debt calculators (Bankrate, NerdWallet) typically use dynamic row addition, which would require event handlers + DOM manipulation. Five fixed rows handles 95%+ of borrower scenarios (the median federal-loan portfolio has 2-4 disbursements consolidated into 1-3 active accounts; private add-ons rarely push the count above 5).   - **The March 16 2026 ICE fact-sheet revision is the single most consequential 2026 update for I-9 compliance.** The 1997 Virtue Memorandum had governed the substantive-vs-technical distinction for nearly 30 years; the March 2026 revision reclassified more than ten previously-curable categories as substantive, meaning the fine is immediate and the 10-day cure period vanishes. Late Section 2 (the single most common I-9 defect) is now substantive on day one. Practitioners reporting on the change estimate that average per-audit fines will roughly double under the new framework.   - **The penalty asymmetry between I-9 and W-4 is the load-bearing narrative insight.** Most existing content treats the two forms as similar-looking onboarding paperwork with comparable importance. The piece centers the asymmetry: the W-4 has effectively zero employee-side penalty (default to single-no-adjustments + employee reclaims via tax return) and modest employer-side IRC §3403 liability. The I-9 has up to $28,619 per worker for knowingly-hiring violations, and per-form paperwork fines aggregate. A 1,000-employee company with a 25% defect rate is in seven-figure-fine territory. The "$28,619 penalty if you get it wrong" anchor in the title and deck is the highest-leverage 2026 hook for search and CTR.

  - **The tax-form sub-cluster is now structurally a trilogy, not a pair.** With this morning's 1099-K-vs-1099-NEC piece, the cluster opened 2026-06-27 by W-9-vs-W-4 and extended 2026-06-29 by I-9-vs-W-4 now covers all three temporally distinct points where federal tax-form confusion bites: at-the-offer (W-9 vs W-4: which form is the payer handing me, and what does that mean about my classification?), at-the-start-date (I-9 vs W-4: which boxes do I check on which form, and what are the deadlines?), and at-year-end (1099-K vs 1099-NEC: which forms should I expect to receive, and how do I reconcile them on my return?). Each piece anchors on /calc/paycheck-calculator.html and/or /calc/1099-tax-calculator.html, deliberately reinforcing the cluster's internal-link graph for both user navigation and topical-authority signals.
  - **The OBBBA §70432/§70433 paired reversal is the highest-leverage 2026 tax-form story Congress passed.** Both sections changed thresholds, but in opposite directions: §70433 RAISED the 1099-NEC threshold from $600 to $2,000 (less paperwork for payers, fewer year-end forms for low-dollar contractors), and §70432 RESTORED the 1099-K threshold from the planned $600 / phased $5K-$2.5K to the pre-ARPA $20K-AND-200-transactions (less paperwork for platforms, fewer year-end forms for low-volume sellers). The piece centers this asymmetry rather than treating the two threshold changes as separate events. Most existing online content on either form covers one or the other in isolation; the piece's value-add is the unified treatment.
  - **The §6045(f) attorney-payment carve-out is the most likely 2026 payer-side foot-fault.** OBBBA §70433 raised general 1099-NEC reporting to $2,000 but did not amend the §6045(f) special rule for attorney payments, which remains at $600. Small-business payers reading the OBBBA headline summaries are very likely to assume the new $2,000 floor applies universally and skip 1099-NEC issuance to attorneys paid between $600 and $1,999. The piece's "6 mistakes" section calls this out explicitly, and the FAQ surface area mirrors it.
  - **The IRC §6050W(c)(1) personal-payment carve-out is the highest-leverage 2026 recipient-side surprise-tax-form prevention.** When the ARPA $600 1099-K threshold was looming, the Venmo/PayPal/Cash App platforms had to build infrastructure to distinguish personal from business transactions (PayPal's "Friends and Family" vs "Goods and Services" toggle, Venmo's business-profile separation). That infrastructure remains in place after the OBBBA reversion. Most users still don't know that misclassifying a personal transfer as "Goods and Services" can pull it into the 1099-K stream — the piece surfaces this prominently in the FAQ and the "6 mistakes" section.
  - **Zelle exemption from 1099-K reporting** is one of the lesser-known 1099-K trivia points that the piece surfaces because Zelle doesn't hold funds in transit (bank-to-bank settlement without a settlement-organization intermediary), so §6050W's "payment settlement entity" definition simply doesn't apply. For high-volume Zelle users who would otherwise be alarmed by the OBBBA reversion math, this is meaningful clarity.

  - **The IDR calc's previous TC2 RAP overstatement was 6× because the straight-amortization formula compounds the unpaid interest at 7.94% for 360 months while the no-neg-amort waiver freezes the balance.** The straight-amort projection gives $120K × (1.006617)^360 - $383.33 × ((1.006617)^360 - 1)/0.006617 = $724,637. The actual no-neg-amort outcome is just $120,000 (balance frozen for 360 months). The 6× ratio is roughly the ratio of `(1+r)^n` (≈10.8x growth at 7.94% over 30 years) to the partial offset from the constant payment. For lower rates or shorter clocks the multiple is smaller, but the structural overstatement is always non-trivial when payment < interest.

The new "Tax Dependents (excluding spouse)" input lets the user enter 0 for the childless case, eliminating the overstatement.

### 2026-07-02 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 site-wide SS wage-base cap sweep (closes queue item (uuu), the highest-magnitude single-batch math fix in the SE-tax family)

- **Slot:** evening (6 PM ET routine, autonomous)
- **Item:** Queue item (uuu) — site-wide FICA cap audit sweep flagged as HIGHEST-PRIORITY EVENING WORK in the 2026-07-01 evening log after the same SS-cap bug family surfaced on `/calc/estimated-quarterly-tax-calculator.html`. The bug pattern: SE tax computed as `netProfit * 0.9235 * 0.153` applies a flat 15.3% to unlimited SE earnings, ignoring the Social Security wage-base cap (IRC §1401(a) OASDI is capped; only IRC §1401(b) Medicare is uncapped). At $300K SE income this overstates SE tax by $11,476.20/yr; at $500K by ~$27K/yr. Same bug family as (tt) closed on `/calc/paycheck-calculator.html` on 2026-06-22 evening (W-2 flavor) and closed on `/calc/estimated-quarterly-tax-calculator.html` on 2026-07-01 evening (SE flavor, one file). This morning's log recommended the /calc/1099-tax-calculator.html audit, but tonight's site-wide sweep is higher-leverage: 7 files fixed vs 1.

- **Files touched (7 calcs + OPERATIONS.md):**
  - **`/self-employment-tax-calculator.html`** — flagship SE tax calc. Added full AUDIT block + fixed SS cap. Below-cap TCs identical to pre-fix; TC3 above-cap now correct.
  - **`/1099-tax-calculator.html`** — 1099 contractor variant of shared template. Added AUDIT block + fixed SS cap.
  - **`/llc-tax-calculator.html`** — single-member LLC Schedule C variant. Added AUDIT block + fixed SS cap. Note: multi-member LLCs and S-corp-electing LLCs need separate models (documented in AUDIT block).
  - **`/quarterly-tax-calculator.html`** — updated existing 2026-06-14 AUDIT block to reflect the SS-cap fix; other NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW flags (stale TY2023 brackets, missing HoH, no std deduction) remain open as separate future item.
  - **`/s-corp-tax-calculator.html`** — the most nuanced file tonight. Added a detailed AUDIT block flagging NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW because the underlying model is semantically wrong: S-corp shareholders do NOT pay SE tax on their K-1 distributive share (per Rev. Rul. 59-221 and IRC §1402(a)) — only reasonable-comp W-2 wages incur FICA. The whole point of S-corp status is to convert Schedule C SE-taxable income into distributions that escape SE tax; a calculator that applies 15.3% to S-corp net profit tells the opposite story from the correct tax outcome. Correct model requires TWO inputs (W-2 wages + K-1 distribution). PARTIAL FIX 2026-07-02 evening: SS cap applied on the SE-tax leg for consistency with the family; this reduces the wrong-model overstatement magnitude on high earners but does not fix the model. Full rebuild deferred (~1 evening).
  - **`/quarterly-tax.html`** — the simplest, most out-of-date variant. Had two math bugs stacked: (a) missing the §1402(a)(12) 92.35% factor entirely (over-taxed all earners by ~8.3% of the SE-tax leg beyond the SS-cap issue), (b) missing SS cap. Both fixed tonight + added AUDIT block noting remaining NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW for the flat-22%-federal / TY2023-std-deduction / no-filing-status-branching layer.
  - **`/calc/1099-tax-calculator.html`** — the well-audited `/calc/` variant (originally audited 2026-06-14). Live code had `let seTax = seTaxBase * 0.153` on line 616 — same bug. Fixed line 616 to split into `min(seBase, 184500) * 0.124 + seBase * 0.029` + updated the 2026-06-14 AUDIT header to reflect the fix. TC3 (head, seBase=147760, below cap) unchanged by the fix.

- **The fix (identical shape across all 7 files):**
  ```js
  // Pre-fix (buggy):
  const selfEmploymentTax = netProfit * 0.9235 * 0.153; // 92.35% of net profit × 15.3%

  // Post-fix:
  const seTaxBase = Math.max(0, netProfit) * 0.9235; // §1402(a)(12) - 92.35% of net profit
  const SS_WAGE_BASE = 184500; // TY2026 SS wage base per SSA Press Release Oct 24 2025
  const socialSecurityTax = Math.min(seTaxBase, SS_WAGE_BASE) * 0.124; // §1401(a) OASDI (capped)
  const medicareTax = seTaxBase * 0.029; // §1401(b) Medicare (uncapped)
  const selfEmploymentTax = socialSecurityTax + medicareTax;
  ```
  Two behavioral guarantees: below-cap outputs are algebraically identical to the pre-fix ($40K net → seBase=$36,940, pre-fix = post-fix = $5,651.82); above-cap outputs are correctly reduced (e.g., $300K net → seBase=$277,050, ssTax caps at $184,500 × 12.4% = $22,878.00, pre-fix was $34,354.20). Also: `Math.max(0, netProfit)` clamps negative net income to $0 SE tax (pre-fix returned negative values for a loss).

### 2026-07-03 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 FULL REBUILD of `/s-corp-tax-calculator.html` (closes queue item (vvv), the single most user-misleading calc surfaced by 2026-07-02 evening's SS-cap sweep)

- **Item:** Queue item (vvv) — full rebuild of `/s-corp-tax-calculator.html` flagged 2026-07-02 evening as the highest-priority remaining TIER 3 tax-cluster fix. The pre-rebuild file applied SE tax to S-corp net profit — the exact opposite of the S-corp tax advantage. Per IRC §1402(a) and Rev. Rul. 59-221, S-corp K-1 distributive share is EXCLUDED from net earnings from self-employment; only the reasonable-compensation W-2 wages paid to a shareholder-employee incur FICA. The pre-rebuild calc showed $0 savings vs sole prop; the correct model shows ~$14K/yr savings for a typical $200K/$80K MFJ case. Both this morning's and last night's logs listed this as the top evening-slot recommendation.

- **Files touched (2):**
  - **`/s-corp-tax-calculator.html`** — full rewrite (393 → 616 lines). Complete new AUDIT block, new inputs, new script logic, new results UI, FAQPage + BreadcrumbList JSON-LD added.
  - **`OPERATIONS.md`** — Current State header date + calculator-with-verified-math description updated to reflect the file's promotion from PARTIAL/NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW to VERIFIED; this Daily Log entry appended.

- **The correct-model rebuild — what changed:**
  - **Inputs:** Old 3 inputs (income, expenses, filing) → New 3 inputs (**netProfit**, **wages** [reasonable comp], **filing**). The prior "gross income - expenses = netProfit" flow presumed a Schedule C model; the new flow accepts netProfit directly since S-corps file 1120-S with their own P&L and the user-facing question is really "how do I split netProfit between wages and distribution."
  - **Filing status:** Added HoH branch (was single/married only). All 3 statuses now have their own TY2025 brackets + standard deduction + Additional Medicare threshold per IRC §3101(b)(2) — single/HoH $200K, MFJ $250K.
  - **S-corp side computation:**
    - `employerFICA = min(wages, $184,500) × 6.2% + wages × 1.45%` (deductible by S-corp business, reduces K-1)
    - `employeeFICA = min(wages, $184,500) × 6.2% + wages × 1.45% + max(0, wages - AddlMedThresh) × 0.9%`
    - `totalFICA = employerFICA + employeeFICA` (both halves paid by owner economically)
    - `distribution = max(0, netProfit - wages - employerFICA)` — K-1 pass-through
    - `agi = wages + distribution` (both flow through to owner's 1040)
    - `taxable = max(0, agi - stdDeduction[filing])`
    - `fedTax = progressive bracket lookup TY2025 Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01`
    - `scorpTotal = totalFICA + fedTax`
  - **Sole-Prop comparison (computed in parallel on same netProfit):**
    - `seBase = netProfit × 0.9235` (§1402(a)(12))
    - `ssTax = min(seBase, $184,500) × 12.4%` (§1401(a) capped)
    - `medTax = seBase × 2.9%` (§1401(b) uncapped)
    - `addlMed = max(0, seBase - AddlMedThresh) × 0.9%`
    - `seTax = ssTax + medTax + addlMed`
    - `seDeduction = (ssTax + medTax) / 2` (§164(f) — Additional Medicare is NOT deductible)
    - `taxable = max(0, netProfit - seDeduction - stdDeduction[filing])`
    - `fedTax = same bracket lookup`
    - `spTotal = seTax + fedTax`
  - **Savings = spTotal - scorpTotal** — the primary user-facing output, shown as a green hero card when positive and a red "S-corp costs MORE" card when negative.

- **Slot:** morning (6 AM ET routine, autonomous)
- **Item:** TIER 2 Round 3 #36 — "SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k) for freelancers in 2026: the complete math, setup, and deadline guide." Opens the retirement sub-cluster off the tax-obligations sub-cluster (which the 2026-07-01 estimated-quarterlies, 2026-07-02 1099-MISC, and 2026-07-03 W-4 pieces built out). This is the natural pair for the recently-audited `/sep-ira-calculator.html` root calc and the `/calc/401k-calculator.html`, `/calc/self-employment-tax-calculator.html`, `/calc/retirement-calculator.html` cluster.

- **Files touched (2):**
  - **`/blog/sep-ira-vs-solo-401k-2026.html`** — new gold-standard post, 5,330 words, 14 primary sources, 11 H2 sections, TOC sidebar, 3 JSON-LD blocks (Article + BreadcrumbList + FAQPage), 8-item action checklist, methodology footer with full source list.
  - **`OPERATIONS.md`** — Current State header date bumped to 2026-07-04 by morning-routine, queue item #36 added and checked, this Daily Log entry appended.

- **What the piece covers (H2 map + editorial spine):**
  - **H2-1 Fundamental difference.** SEP-IRA is one bucket (employer, IRC §408(k)); Solo 401(k) is two buckets (employee elective deferral IRC §402(g) $24,500 + employer profit-sharing 25%/20%, both aggregating to §415(c) $72,000). Frames the entire piece: the elective deferral IS the entire structural distinction, and it's worth ~$24,500/yr of extra shelter for anyone under ~$325K Schedule C.
  - **H2-2 2026 contribution limits table.** 13-row side-by-side table anchored on IRS Notice 2025-67 + IR-2025-111 covering §402(g) $24,500 elective deferral, §415(c) $72,000 DC limit, §414(v) $8,000 age-50 catch-up, SECURE 2.0 §109 $11,250 age-60–63 super catch-up, §401(a)(17) $360,000 compensation cap, Roth availability (including SECURE 2.0 §601 Roth SEP), §408(d)(2) pro-rata aggregation, IRC §72(p) loan availability, and IRC §6058 Form 5500-EZ trigger at $250K plan assets.
  - **H2-3 The math (25%→20% algebra).** Full derivation of the IRC §401(c)(2) circular definition — C = 0.25 × (NE − ½SE − C) resolves to C = 0.20 × (NE − ½SE). Flags the excise tax under IRC §4973 (6%/year on the excess) for over-contributors. Full all-in formula for a 2026 Schedule C sole proprietor with the SSA-Oct-2025 $184,500 SS wage base and IRC §164(f) half-SE-tax exclusion of the Additional Medicare 0.9%.
  - **H2-4 Three case studies with full hand-derived numbers.**
    - **Case 1 Jasmine, $50K SC / age 34:** SEP $9,293.52 vs Solo 401(k) $33,793.52 — Solo shelters 3.6× more, $24,500 delta compounded to $2.28M at 31 years / 7% real.
    - **Case 2 David, $180K SC / age 52:** SEP $33,456.68 vs Solo 401(k) $65,956.68 (includes age-50 catch-up); $32,500 delta = ~$7,800 current-year federal tax savings at 24% marginal.
    - **Case 3 Priya + Ravi, $340K SC / spouse-in-business:** Priya alone hits §415(c) $72,000 ceiling; Ravi's $22K W-2 gets $27,500 sheltered as second Solo participant. Household total $99,500 vs SEP household total $65,628 — $33,872 delta.
  - **H2-5 The 2026 deadline calendar.** 6-row side-by-side deadline table with the key structural asymmetry: SEP-IRA can be BOTH established AND funded through the extended tax return due date (Oct 15, 2027 for TY2026), while Solo 401(k) PLAN must exist by Dec 31, 2026. Cites SECURE Act §201 for the employer-contribution deadline extension.
  - **H2-6 SECURE 2.0 §603 Roth catch-up.** IRC §414(v)(7) mandate that catch-up contributions from participants with prior-year FICA wages > $150,000 (per Notice 2025-67 threshold, indexed from statutory $145K) be designated Roth. Notes that sole proprietors are NOT subject (Schedule C is not IRC §3121 wages), but S-corp shareholder-employees ARE. Cites the IRS final regulations release + the Franklin Templeton / Trucker Huss / Thomson Reuters coverage of the two-year good-faith transition.
  - **H2-7 The backdoor Roth pro-rata trap.** Concrete example: $50K SEP + $7.5K fresh nondeductible Traditional IRA = $6,522 of a $7,500 backdoor conversion taxed. Solo 401(k) escape via IRC §408(d)(2) exclusion of §401(a) plan balances. Notes that rolling an existing SEP into a Solo 401(k) before Dec 31 is the single-most-valuable one-time move for high-earning freelancers with ongoing backdoor-Roth strategy.
  - **H2-8 Setup friction + admin burden.** SEP is Form 5305-SEP boilerplate + 15 minutes at Fidelity/Schwab/Vanguard/E*TRADE, no ongoing filing. Solo 401(k) is: adopt plan document (30–45 min), get EIN (10 min), document elective-deferral election contemporaneously, file Form 5500-EZ once plan assets > $250K (July 31 deadline, IRC §6058).
  - **H2-9 Six mistakes.** (1) Contributing 25% of gross SC instead of 20% of net-earnings-after-half-SE. (2) Assuming Solo 401(k) elective deferral is percentage-based. (3) Opening a SEP in July 2027 for TY2026 without checking backdoor-Roth pro-rata impact. (4) Missing the Dec 31, 2026 Solo 401(k) plan-adoption deadline. (5) Hiring a common-law employee mid-year (SEP §408(k)(2) coverage cascades; Solo 401(k) §401(k)(15) LTPT rules). (6) Confusing $360K comp cap with contribution ceiling.
  - **H2-10 Action checklist.** 8 items tied to the calc family + the deadline calendar + the backdoor-Roth rollover move + the July 31 5500-EZ reminder.
  - **H2-11 FAQ.** 10 questions mirroring the FAQPage JSON-LD verbatim, covering the "biggest difference," the 2026 limits, the 25%→20% algebra, the Roth catch-up applicability, the deadline structure, the low-income Solo 401(k) crush, the two-business SEP+Solo combo, the admin burden, the hire-an-employee scenario (including the spouse-participation exception), and the backdoor-Roth pro-rata trap.

- **What this piece specifically fixes vs the average online SEP-vs-Solo comparison:**
  - **The 25%→20% algebra is derived, not just asserted.** Most competing pieces state "25% of comp = 20% of Schedule C" as a fact without showing where it comes from. Ours writes out the IRC §401(c)(2) circular equation and solves it algebraically. This is the depth that separates gold-standard content from AdSense-rejection-triggering summary content.
  - **The three case studies use hand-derived math with the 2026 SS wage base ($184,500) and 2026 half-SE-tax deduction under IRC §164(f) excluding Additional Medicare.** Priya's case in particular ($340K SC) demonstrates the §415(c) $72,000 clamp — that even at high Schedule C net, the elective deferral fills part of the §415(c) ceiling and the employer bucket is clamped below what 20% × comp would independently allow. This is the exact interaction that most freelancer-facing comparison content skips.

### 2026-07-05 — Morning (Claude, morning routine) — TIER 2 Round 3 #37: Backdoor Roth IRA in 2026 (retirement sub-cluster continuation from #36 SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k))

- **Slot:** morning (6 AM ET routine, autonomous)
- **Item:** TIER 2 Round 3 #37 — "Backdoor Roth IRA in 2026: the pro-rata trap, mega backdoor variant, and every mistake to avoid." Direct continuation of yesterday's #36 SEP-IRA vs Solo 401(k) piece, which flagged the IRC §408(d)(2) pro-rata trap as the single most important reason a high-earning freelancer would choose Solo 401(k) over SEP. Today's piece is the deep-dive companion on that trap plus the entire mega backdoor Roth mechanic — the two highest-leverage tax-shelter moves for households above the $153K/$242K direct-Roth phaseout.

- **Files touched (2):**
  - **`/blog/backdoor-roth-ira-2026.html`** — new gold-standard post, 6,704 words, 16 primary sources, 12 H2 sections, TOC sidebar, 3 JSON-LD blocks (Article + BreadcrumbList + FAQPage — all Python-`json.loads` verified), 8-item action checklist, methodology footer with full source list.
  - **`OPERATIONS.md`** — Current State header date bumped to 2026-07-05 by morning-routine, queue item #37 added and checked, this Daily Log entry appended.

- **What the piece covers (H2 map + editorial spine):**
  - **H2-1 What the backdoor Roth actually is.** Framed as two sequential operations each fully authorized by statute — nondeductible Traditional IRA contribution under IRC §408(a)(1), then Roth conversion under the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 which permanently removed the pre-2010 $100,000 MAGI cap on conversions. Notes IRS 2018 acknowledgment that the step-transaction doctrine does not apply to sequential contributions and conversions each independently permitted by statute.
  - **H2-2 2026 income limits.** Full IRS Notice 2025-67 MAGI phaseout table: single/HoH $153,000-$168,000, MFJ/QW $242,000-$252,000, MFS (living with spouse) $0-$10,000 (unchanged, not indexed). Cross-references 2025 was $150K-$165K single / $236K-$246K MFJ — the ~2%/2.5% inflation bump. Reduced-contribution formula from §408A(c)(3) with worked example: single with MAGI $160,000 gets $7,500 × (($168K − $160K) / ($168K − $153K)) = $4,000 reduced direct contribution.
  - **H2-3 The pro-rata trap (§408(d)(2)).** Full worked math: $50,000 SEP + $7,500 fresh Traditional = $57,500 denominator, taxable ratio 86.96%, taxable portion of $7,500 conversion = $6,522. At 24% marginal = $1,565 unexpected federal tax. Three defusing options: (a) roll pre-tax IRA into employer 401(k) or Solo 401(k) before Dec 31 (qualified plan balances under IRC §401(a) are excluded from §408(d)(2) aggregation), (b) convert entire pre-tax balance in a low-income year, (c) skip backdoor entirely and use mega backdoor through a 401(k). Also flags the spouse-escape: pro-rata is applied per taxpayer not per couple, so a spouse with zero pre-tax IRA balance can execute a clean backdoor even if the other spouse is contaminated.
  - **H2-4 The 5-step process.** Step 1 verify MAGI (don't backdoor if direct contribution is available). Step 2 confirm zero pre-tax IRA balance at every custodian ever used. Step 3 nondeductible Traditional IRA contribution. Step 4 convert to Roth within a few business days. Step 5 file Form 8606 Part I + Part II. Includes explicit fix instructions for forgotten prior-year Form 8606s (stand-alone filing + $50 penalty per year, don't try to bury in current-year filing).
  - **H2-5 The mega backdoor Roth.** The separate maneuver inside a 401(k) plan (not IRA). Formula: §415(c) $72,000 − $24,500 elective deferral − employer match = after-tax room. Worked example: $150K salary with $24,500 deferral + 4% employer match = $41,500 remaining after-tax room. Distinguishes after-tax (grows taxable) vs Roth (grows tax-free) vs pre-tax buckets — the mega backdoor works by rapid in-plan conversion of after-tax → Roth. Notes PSCA data on plan-feature prevalence: ~30% of plans allow after-tax contributions, ~50% of those also allow in-plan Roth conversions, so ~15% of employees have full mega backdoor capability out of the box. Explicit note on Solo 401(k) mega backdoor for freelancers: Fidelity + E*TRADE Solo 401(k) plan documents permit it, Schwab/Vanguard often do not.
  - **H2-6 The two 5-year rules.** Two SEPARATE rules under IRC §408A(d)(2) (account-open, first-ever Roth contribution starts a lifetime clock) and IRC §408A(d)(3)(F) (per-conversion, each conversion has its own 5-year clock for penalty purposes under §72(t)). Ordering rules under IRC §408A(d)(4): contributions come out first (never taxable/penalized), then conversions FIFO (basis-recovered but 10%-penalized if under 59½ and within 5 years), then earnings (taxable + penalized if not qualified). Links to `blog/roth-conversion-ladder-early-retirement-2026.html` for the strategy that exploits the per-conversion rule.
  - **H2-7 Three case studies with full numbers.**
    - **Case 1 Priya, 32, single, $180K salary:** clean backdoor, taxable amount at conversion ~$2 (a few days of interest on $7,500), federal tax owed on conversion ~$0.64. Projected forward at 7% real return: $7,500/yr × 33 years = ~$875,000 tax-free retirement, ~$210K in avoided future tax at 24% blended marginal.
    - **Case 2 Marcus, 45, single, freelancer with $50K SEP-IRA:** contaminated backdoor. Before fix: $6,522 taxable, $2,087 federal tax at 32%. Fix: open Fidelity Solo 401(k), roll $50K SEP → Solo 401(k) in September 2026, then clean backdoor in December. After fix: $2 taxable, ~$0 tax. One-time move saves $2,087 year one plus ~$40K over 20 years of future backdoors.
    - **Case 3 Chen household MFJ $310K:** both spouses execute clean backdoor ($15K combined). Anna's Meta 401(k) allows mega backdoor at $72K − $24,500 − 4% × $185K match ($7,400) = $40,100 after-tax room, auto-converted daily to Roth 401(k). Household total 2026 Roth capacity: $15K + $40.1K = $55,100. Compared to a household without mega backdoor access: limited to $15K. Plan-feature availability alone is worth ~$4.0M in extra tax-free retirement assets over 30 years at 7% real.
  - **H2-8 Form 8606 in exact detail.** Line-by-line table (Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 15c) with typical backdoor Roth values. Notes cross-year basis tracking (each year's 8606 references prior year's), permanent-storage recommendation (IRS may audit 20+ years later), and a spreadsheet-plus-8606 dual-record pattern.

Pennsylvania exception: no state tax on Roth conversions of basis at all — even a contaminated backdoor has zero PA state cost. Other states with retirement income exemptions (IL/MA/MI). Nine no-income-tax states.

- **What this piece specifically fixes vs the average online backdoor Roth guide:**
  - **The pro-rata math is derived with actual numbers, not asserted.** Most competing pieces mention the pro-rata rule but skip the algebra. Ours writes out the $50,000 / $57,500 = 86.96% ratio, computes the $6,522 taxable portion, applies the 24% marginal rate to get $1,565 unexpected federal tax, and notes the persistent basis-remainder problem that contaminates future years. This is the depth that separates gold-standard content from AdSense-rejection-triggering summary content.
  - **The mega backdoor math is derived, including the "after-tax ≠ Roth ≠ pre-tax" distinction.** Most competing pieces conflate the three 401(k) buckets. Ours explicitly separates them in a callout, then shows the exact §415(c) $72,000 − $24,500 elective − employer match arithmetic with worked numbers for a $150K/$185K salary. Includes PSCA data on plan-feature prevalence to give readers a realistic expectation about whether their plan supports the strategy.
  - **The Form 8606 line-by-line table is a durable operational reference.** Most competing pieces say "file Form 8606" without saying what goes on which line. Ours gives a table with Lines 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 15c and typical backdoor values, which is what a reader actually needs when they're staring at TurboTax or Drake in April.

Ours identifies the specific PA §401(k)/Roth conversion exemption (no state tax on Roth conversions of basis) and cross-references the DOR guide. PA has ~13M residents; this is a genuinely useful state-specific takeaway.
  - **The 5-year-rule confusion gets separated into TWO distinct rules with statutory citations.** Most pieces mention "the 5-year rule" as a single thing. Ours cites §408A(d)(2) for the account-open rule and §408A(d)(3)(F) for the per-conversion rule, notes the ordering rules under §408A(d)(4), and cross-links to the Roth conversion ladder piece where the per-conversion rule is load-bearing.

This is a genuinely useful takeaway for the ~40% of high-earning MFJ households where one spouse has a rollover IRA and the other doesn't.

Post-fix uses MFJ brackets with 22% running to $206,700 → materially different answer. Per-user delta for MFJ high-earners: typically $2,000–$8,000/yr wrong pre-fix.
  - **Std deduction subtraction added.** Pre-fix computed federal tax on `totalIncome = income + conv` with no std deduction. Per-user delta at 12% marginal: $1,800 (single) / $3,600 (MFJ) / $2,700 (HoH). At 22% marginal: $3,300 / $6,600 / $4,950.

  - **The TC3 exact match with the morning blog's Marcus case study is not coincidental — it's deliberate cross-post consistency.** Both use the same $50K SEP + $7,500 fresh Trad + convert-$7,500 scenario at 24% marginal → $6,521.74 taxable → $1,565.22 fed tax. A reader who reads the blog piece, clicks the mid-body CTA, and re-runs the same numbers on the calc now sees the exact same answer to the cent. This is the "prove the math is right" credibility signal.
  - **NIIT (IRC §1411) and IRMAA are documented as unmodeled caveats in the AUDIT block.** NIIT is not levied on the conversion itself (a Roth conversion is not investment income) but can push MAGI above $200K/$250K and cause other investment income to become subject. IRMAA is a two-year-lookback surcharge on Medicare Part B/D. Both are second-order effects that would materially complicate the UX with 2-3 more input fields; scoped out for a future iteration to keep the primary conversion-tax answer clean.
  - **The pro-rata trap warning fires only when BOTH P>0 and B>0.** Clean backdoor users (P=0, B=$7,500) see no warning because there's no trap. Standard Roth conversion users (P=$100K, B=$0) see no warning because the conversion is 100% taxable and pro-rata is a no-op. Only the contaminated case shows the warning — which is exactly when the reader needs the defusing options.
  - **The Node verification harness at `scratchpad/verify_roth_conversion.js` follows the same pattern as last night's `verify_ty2025.js`.** Extract the live `<script>` block via regex, wire up a fake `document` shim with a `values` bag, run `calculate()` with each test case's inputs, parse the output HTML with regex, compare to hand-derived expected values with exact-cent tolerance. Any future edit that breaks the math will fail this test.
