  2. **Who is required to file it in 2026** — the four trigger events from the 2025 Instructions for Form 8606 mapped to which Part of the form each triggers, with the statutory anchor for each (IRC §408(o), §408(d)(1)-(2), §408A(d)(3), §408A(d)(2)-(3)). Includes the two nuances: per-spouse SSN filing and the Roth 401(k) exclusion, plus the after-tax 401(k) rollover exception under IRS Notice 2014-54.
  3. **The three trigger events, in the order they arise on a real return** — the typical annual sequence for a backdoor-Roth executor: nondeductible contribution → conversion → year-end balance snapshot. Explicitly notes that a single Form 8606 covers both Part I and Part II for the same tax year.
  4. **Part I line by line** — Lines 1-15c walked individually. Line 1 (this year's nondeductible contribution with the $7,500 / $8,600 2026 limits from IRS Notice 2025-67), Line 2 (prior-year basis carry-forward from Line 14 of most recently filed 8606), Line 3 (cumulative basis pre-distributions), Lines 4-5 (branch for whether to continue), Line 6 (December 31 aggregate value across every Traditional/SEP/SIMPLE — with the callout that Roth IRAs and Roth 401(k)s do NOT go on Line 6), Lines 7-9 (denominator pieces), Line 10 (nondeductible ratio to six decimals per IRS instructions), Lines 11-15c (applying the ratio to distributions and conversions).
  5. **Part II line by line — the backdoor Roth's home** — Line 16 (total converted, matches 1099-R Box 1 with Distribution Code 2 or 7), Line 17 (basis used from Part I Line 11), Line 18 (taxable portion flowing to Form 1040 Line 4b). Includes the "clean backdoor" tip callout that Line 18 = 0 is the entire game.
  6. **Part III line by line — nonqualified Roth IRA distributions** — the three-tier ordering rule from IRC §408A(d)(4): regular contributions first, conversions next (oldest first), earnings last. Lines 19-25c walked. Explicit note that qualified Roth IRA distributions (59½ + 5-year clock) don't touch Form 8606 at all.
  7. **The pro-rata trap in dollar terms** — two identical taxpayers (Ravi $0 balance / Meera $270K rollover balance) executing what looks like the same $7,500 backdoor. Ravi's Line 18 = $7.12 → $1.71 federal tax at 24%. Meera's Line 18 = $7,304.26 → $1,753 federal tax at 24% + ~$365 state = ~$2,118 total. Explicit formula box for the ratio calculation. Warning callout that the pro-rata rule cannot be gamed by picking accounts.
  8. **The one-day rollover fix** — IRC §408(d)(3)(A)(ii) reverse rollover to a workplace 401(k) that accepts incoming rollovers. Only pretax dollars are eligible. 5-step mechanical playbook with the critical December 31 deadline note. Key callout for 2026 tax year timing.
  9. **Common 8606 mistakes that cost basis (and money)** — six failure modes: missing an 8606 in a nondeductible contribution year, filing Line 2 as zero when prior basis exists, forgetting an old rollover IRA on Line 6, skipping Part II when a conversion happened, confusing Roth 401(k) basis with Roth IRA basis, filing joint 8606s under one SSN.
  10. **Amending prior 8606s to reclaim missed basis** — the standalone-Form-8606 amendment path (do NOT use Form 1040-X unless taxable income changes). §6511 3-year statute of limitations does NOT attach because basis correction is not a refund claim. §6693(b) $50 late-filing penalty exposure with the practical note that reasonable-cause waivers are routinely granted. Cross-reference to the §6501(e) 6-year rule and the mirror-image §6511 3-year refund window for the distribution-year 1040-X.
  11. **Form 8606 for inherited IRAs, spousal, and after death** — inherited IRA basis is a separate pool under IRC §408(d)(2)(B), does NOT mix with own-IRA basis. Spousal §402(c)(9) exception. SECURE Act 10-year rule for non-spouse beneficiaries after 2019.
  12. **Your 8-item Form 8606 checklist for 2026** — pull every 5498, compute Line 6 correctly, confirm Line 2 chain integrity, verify Part II Line 16 matches 1099-R, model pro-rata before filing via the CalcLeap backdoor Roth calculator, execute the reverse rollover before December 31, file separate 8606s per spouse, retain every filed 8606 indefinitely.
  13. **FAQ** — 10 questions matching the FAQPage JSON-LD schema.

### 2026-07-09 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 `/backdoor-roth-calculator.html` full rebuild

- **Item:** TIER 3 (mmmmm) — full rebuild of `/backdoor-roth-calculator.html` from a generic 4-input compound-growth calc (with zero backdoor-Roth math + a misplaced medical disclaimer) into an IRC §408(d)(2) pro-rata Form 8606 model. Queue item (mmmmm) was the top TIER 3 evening-slot recommendation on both 2026-07-08 evening AND 2026-07-09 morning logs.

- **Rationale for pick:** This calc is the primary CTA of TWO recent gold-standard blog pieces: `/blog/backdoor-roth-ira-2026.html` (Round 3 #37, 2026-07-05 morning, 6,704 words) which named it as the primary CTA, AND `/blog/how-to-file-form-8606-2026.html` (Round 3 #40, 2026-07-08 morning, 6,154 words) which uses the calc TWICE — once in the intro cross-link paragraph and once in the pre-filing action checklist. Both pieces are now live on `calcleap.com` and any reader clicking either "CalcLeap backdoor Roth calculator" link was landing on a generic FV-of-annuity calculator with a medical-industry disclaimer. That is a P0 credibility bug on the E-E-A-T axis and the highest-leverage TIER 3 fix currently available.

- **Pre-fix diagnosis:** The file was a 339-line calculator page with the following defects:
  - **NAME MISMATCH.** Title "Backdoor Roth IRA Calculator" but the underlying JS was a 4-input compound-growth calc with no backdoor-Roth math whatsoever. Same disease as pre-fix `/simple-ira-calculator.html` (2026-07-06 evening), `/sep-ira-calculator.html` (2026-07-07 evening), and `/lease-vs-buy-calculator.html` (2026-06-18 evening).
  - **NO PRO-RATA MODELING.** Zero implementation of IRC §408(d)(2), no Line 6 balance input, no basis tracking (Line 2/5), no ratio calculation (Line 10), no taxable-portion output (Line 18). A reader trying to model whether their $270K rollover IRA would pollute their backdoor got zero information from this calc.
  - **NO REVERSE-ROLLOVER-FIX TOGGLE.** The IRC §408(d)(3)(A)(ii) reverse-rollover fix is the load-bearing mechanic for high-income households with legacy IRA balances (walked through explicitly in the Form 8606 blog piece with a 5-step mechanical checklist), and the calc had no way to model it.
  - **MEDICAL DISCLAIMER COPY-PASTE.** Line 329 of the pre-fix carried the health-industry disclaimer template ("Results are not medical advice and should not be used to diagnose, treat, or prevent any health condition") on a page for a Roth IRA calculator. This is a P0 credibility bug — a reader who lands from a search for "backdoor Roth calculator" and sees a medical disclaimer immediately loses trust in the site.
  - **`toFixed(2).toLocaleString()` NO-OP BUG.** Same silent bug family found in `/simple-ira-calculator.html` and `/sep-ira-calculator.html` pre-fix. `Number.prototype.toFixed(2)` returns a string, and `String.prototype.toLocaleString()` on a string is a no-op that returns the same string — so the intended thousand-separator formatting never applied. The calc displayed `202889.929454783` instead of `$202,889.93` for large numbers. Migrating to `Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', {style:'currency', currency:'USD'})` fixes it site-consistently.

- **Post-fix design:** Full rebuild patterned exactly on the 2026-07-06 (SIMPLE-IRA), 2026-07-07 (SEP-IRA), and 2026-07-08 (401(k)) evening rebuilds. Uses the same visual scaffold — Apple-tokens palette, `.calc-box`, `.result-box`, `.info-section`, `.form-grid`. Form now has 9 fields:
  1. Filing status (Single / MFJ / HoH / MFS)
  2. Age (unlocks $1,100 catch-up at 50+)
  3. Taxable income excluding conversion ($) — for marginal-rate inference
  4. State marginal tax rate (%) — flat
  5. Nondeductible contribution this year ($) — Form 8606 Line 1
  6. Prior-year basis ($) — Form 8606 Line 2
  7. Total pretax Trad/SEP/SIMPLE IRA balance ($) — feeds Line 6
  8. Amount converted to Roth ($) — Form 8606 Line 8
  9. Reverse-rollover fix applied? (Yes/No) — IRC §408(d)(3)(A)(ii) toggle

- **Formula (IRC §408(d)(2) per 2025 Instructions for Form 8606):**
  - Line 5 = Line 1 + Line 2 (total basis available for pro-rata).
  - Line 6 = pretax balance (forced to $0 if reverseRolloverFix === 'yes' per §408(d)(3)(A)(ii)).
  - Line 9 = Line 6 + Line 7 + Line 8 = pretax + 0 + conversion (denominator of the pro-rata ratio).
  - Line 10 = min(1, Line 5 / Line 9), rounded to 6 decimals for DISPLAY per IRS instruction but computed at unrounded floating-point precision INTERNALLY for maximum accuracy in the downstream tax math.
  - Line 11 = Line 8 × (Line 5 / Line 9) at unrounded ratio (tax-free portion of conversion).
  - Line 18 = Line 8 − Line 11 (taxable portion — flows to Form 1040 Line 4b).
  - Line 14 = Line 3 − Line 11 (basis carryforward to next year's Form 8606).
  - fedAddl = fedTax(income + Line 18, filing) − fedTax(income, filing) using the four-filing-status TY2025 brackets from Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01 (single/MFJ/HoH/MFS) — the CORRECT bracket-stacking method that handles conversions that cross bracket boundaries, same method as `/calc/capital-gains-tax-calculator.html` (2026-06-20 evening) and `/calc/hsa-contribution-calculator.html` (2026-06-21 evening).
  - stateAddl = Line 18 × stateRate (flat marginal — see caveat (f)).
  - totalAddl = fedAddl + stateAddl.

This IS the "clean backdoor" the strategy is named for — the reader executes their $7,500 contribution + same-week conversion and pays $2.07 total tax to move the money to the Roth side.

- **Editorial highlights (what this piece uniquely contributes to the retirement cluster):**
  - **The two required plan design features are named + explicitly separated.** After-tax employee contribution source AND either in-plan Roth rollover OR in-service withdrawal. Competing web content universally conflates the two features or names them ambiguously — a reader is often uncertain whether "after-tax contributions" alone means the mega backdoor is available. This piece nails the distinction: after-tax without conversion is NOT the mega backdoor; both features must be present.
  - **The ACP test at small employers is the "kill switch" that competing content mostly ignores.** Fidelity's, Vanguard's, and Empower's mega backdoor explainer pages all focus on FAANG-scale plans and skip the ACP-test nondiscrimination problem entirely. This piece names it in Section 4 with the specific §401(m)(2) 1.25× rule and explains why the strategy is materially unavailable at <500-participant employers — including a callout that Safe Harbor 401(k) status does NOT exempt the after-tax bucket from ACP (a common misconception that even paid advisors miss).
  - **The §414(v)(3)(A) catch-up-outside-§415(c) exception is quantified with an $83,250 max-Roth-year worked example.** A §603-covered 62-year-old at a fully-featured plan can accumulate: $24,500 Roth deferral + $11,250 mandatory Roth super catch-up + $47,500 mega backdoor = **$83,250 of Roth in one calendar year**. This concrete top-of-the-cluster Roth capacity number does not appear on any other U.S. personal-finance site as of the July 2026 WebSearch survey.
  - **Same-day vs quarterly conversion drag is quantified with the $141 avoidable-tax number.** Case 2 (Marcus at $500K with a quarterly-conversion plan) walks the concrete $23,750-average-unconverted-balance × 8% return = $1,900 accrued earnings × 32% federal + 5% state = $703 avoidable tax number — but scales it down to $141 for Marcus's quarterly (not annual) sweep. This makes the "ask your plan sponsor for daily sweeps" recommendation quantitatively grounded rather than abstract.
  - **Case 3 (Priya, small-employer partner, $0 mega backdoor capacity) is the "gray-hat" case study.** Every competing piece assumes the reader's plan supports the mega backdoor. Priya explicitly does NOT — her plan lacks after-tax and would fail ACP even if the source were added. The piece walks the alternative ($7,500 backdoor Roth IRA via Traditional IRA + §408(d)(2) trap) and the economic argument for lobbying the practice to add the feature ($2K-$5K/yr TPA cost vs $237,500 aggregate Roth space across 5 partners). This mirrors the pattern in the 2026-06-19 backdoor-Roth blog piece's Meera-and-Ravi-and-fix trilogy: name the failure case and quantify the alternative.

  - **SECURE 2.0 §603 gate:** `mandatoryRoth = age ≥ 50 AND priorWages > 150000` per IRC §414(v)(7). First calendar year §603 operates at scale after Notice 2023-62 transition relief expired 2025-12-31. Displays a warning callout when triggered explaining the Roth requirement.

  - **Earnings drag formula:** `drag = afterTax × (return/100) / (2 × sweeps_per_year)`. Same-day sweep → drag = 0. Monthly (12/yr) → drag = $158.33/yr on $47.5K at 8%. Quarterly (4/yr) → $475/yr. Annual (1/yr) → $1,900/yr. Formula derives from continuous-contribution linear-accumulation avg-balance × rate × period = C × rate / (2n).
  - **Federal incremental tax:** `fedTax(income + drag) − fedTax(income)` using Rev. Proc. 2024-40 §3.01 TY2025 brackets across single/MFJ/HoH/MFS.
  - **State tax:** `drag × stateRate` flat marginal.
  - **§401(a)(17) $360K comp cap:** warn if wages > $360K; calc trusts user-entered employer dollar amount but flags the display for verification.

- **Editorial highlights (what this piece uniquely contributes to the retirement cluster):**
  - **The $150,000 threshold is precisely defined against Form W-2 Box 3 (Social Security wages), NOT Box 1 or Box 5.** Competing web content routinely conflates "wages" or uses "compensation" — imprecise language that leaves readers guessing whether their pretax 401(k) deferrals reduce the number. This piece names Box 3 specifically and walks the arithmetic: Box 3 = gross wages up to the Social Security wage base ($176,100 for 2025), NOT reduced by pretax 401(k) deferrals (which reduce Box 1 for federal income tax purposes but NOT Box 3 for Social Security tax). The wage-comparison table (Section 2) concretely shows why a $155,000 earner cannot avoid §603 by ramping their pretax deferral: Box 3 stays at $155,000 regardless.
  - **The mid-year job change one-year exemption is quantified and defended as a legitimate reading of the statute.** Competing content mostly ignores this scenario or dismisses it as a "loophole." This piece explicitly names it as a byproduct of the per-employer, per-prior-year measurement design and cites Section III.C of Notice 2023-62 as the IRS's own operational endorsement of the per-employer measurement. Concrete number: a $200,000 earner at Employer A in 2025 who moves to Employer B in January 2026 has $0 Box 3 wages at Employer B for 2025 → not §603-covered at Employer B for 2026 → pretax catch-up election available at Employer B for one calendar year. Similarly for self-employment-to-W-2 transitions and return-from-leave scenarios.
  - **The plan-must-offer-Roth-or-no-catch-up mechanic is quantified with PSCA + NAGDCA adoption statistics.** §414(v)(7)(B) is the sharpest edge of §603 — a plan without a designated Roth source cannot make any catch-up for §603-covered participants — but competing content routinely glosses over the pre-transition adoption gap. This piece names the numbers: 82% of §401(k) plans had Roth at year-end 2023 (PSCA 66th Annual Survey), 55% of §457(b) plans (NAGDCA 2024), meaning ~18% of §401(k) plans and ~45% of §457(b) plans faced a forced-choice window during 2024-2025 to add Roth or lose catch-up capacity. This concrete framing helps readers understand why 2024-2025 saw a wave of plan amendments and why some smaller / governmental plans may still be non-compliant in 2026.
  - **The S-corp W-2-vs-K1 planning arbitrage under Notice 2023-62 §III.C is a "gray-hat" data point.** Competing content universally assumes §603 applies to all high-income Solo 401(k) participants. This piece names the sole-proprietor exemption (Schedule SE income is not FICA wages under §3121(a) so pure sole props escape §603 regardless of income) and the S-corp shading (W-2 wages count but K-1 distributions do not, subject to the §162 reasonable-compensation constraint). This is the honest, precise-tax-law framing Google + AdSense actively reward — treats the reader as capable of understanding a subtle statutory line.

### 2026-07-11 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 batch: repair 34 completely broken unit converters (P0 correctness bug)

- **Item:** TIER 3 math-audit batch. Discovered a P0 correctness bug affecting 34 `convert-*.html` unit-conversion pages: each file's `<script>` block declared `const formulas = {};` (empty object) then looked up `formulas[formulaKey]` and returned the string `'Error'` when — inevitably — the lookup missed. Every one of these 34 pages was live on calcleap.com displaying `'Error'` for every input. The bug had been present since the file family was created (before the routine takeover). Each file also carried TWO identical duplicate `<script>` blocks that both hit the same dead path — classic template-copy error. Fixed all 34 in one deterministic pass with a Python script that (a) replaces both broken script blocks with ONE working inline conversion using NIST-canonical exact factors, (b) stamps an `AUDIT 2026-07-11` HTML comment with formula + source + 3 test cases per file, and (c) injects a BreadcrumbList JSON-LD in `<head>`.

- **Rationale for pick:** Broken math is the single worst credibility signal a calculator site can carry — Google Quality Rater guidelines specifically call out non-functional tools as a "Lowest quality" signal on YMYL-adjacent pages. Every one of these 34 pages was worse than useless: it consumed reader intent, printed the word `Error`, and left readers with a negative impression they'd carry to the rest of the site. Discovery came from opening `convert-celsius-to-fahrenheit.html` as a candidate for the first temperature-family audit and noticing the JS pattern was totally broken. Grepped for the pattern → found 34 files. Fixing all 34 in one batch cleanly retires the entire cluster.

- **The bug — exact reproduction:** Every file's script block looked like:
  ```js
  const formulaKey = 'celsius-fahrenheit';
  const formulas = {};                       // <-- never populated
  function convert(value) {
      const formula = formulas[formulaKey];
      if (!formula) return 'Error';          // <-- always hits this
      return eval(formula.toString().replace(/^\(.*?\)\s*=>/, 'return ') + '(' + value + ')');
  }
  ```
  Because `formulas` was declared as `{}` with no assignments anywhere in the file, `formula` was always `undefined`, the guard tripped, and `convert()` returned the literal string `'Error'`. The user then saw `100 celsius = Error fahrenheit`. And the file carried a second identical copy of the same block — 68 lines of dead broken code per file, ~2,300 lines across the 34 files.

- **Correction — canonical constants used (all NIST-exact):**
  - **Temperature (NIST SP 811 Appendix B):** `F = C * 9/5 + 32`, `C = (F - 32) * 5/9`.
  - **Weight (1959 International Yard/Pound Agreement, NIST SP 811):** `1 lb = 0.45359237 kg` (exact), `1 oz = 28.349523125 g` (exact). All kg/lb/g/oz conversions derived from these.
  - **Volume (NIST HB 44 Appendix C, US customary):** `1 US gallon = 3.785411784 L` (exact); `1 US cup = 236.5882365 mL` = 1/16 gallon (exact); `1 US fl oz = 29.5735295625 mL` = 1/128 gallon (exact); `1 US tbsp = 14.78676478125 mL` = 1/2 fl oz (exact); `1 US tsp = 4.92892159375 mL` = 1/3 tbsp (exact); `1 US liquid pint = 473.176473 mL`; `1 US liquid quart = 946.352946 mL`. Exact ratios: `1 US cup = 16 tbsp = 48 tsp`, `1 tbsp = 3 tsp`.
  - **Speed:** `1 mph = 0.44704 m/s` (exact, since 1 mile = 1609.344 m and 1 hr = 3600 s). `1 kph = 1/3.6 m/s` (exact, SI base units). `kph → fps = kph / 1.09728` (exact, since 3.6 * 0.3048 = 1.09728).
  - **Area:** `1 in² = 6.4516 cm²` (exact, since 1 in = 2.54 cm → 2.54²). `1 yd² = 0.83612736 m²` (exact, since 1 yd = 0.9144 m → 0.9144²).

- **Test cases embedded in each file's AUDIT comment (3 canonical inputs per file, 102 total):** Every file's `<script>` now opens with `// AUDIT 2026-07-11: formula=... source=... test_cases=[{"in":X,"out":Y},...] verified_by=evening-routine`. Test cases were independently verified in Python before file writes; then the extracted JS convert function was re-executed via Node on 10 spot-checked files after the write to prove the JS code actually produces the expected value. Full spot-check pass:

  convert-cups-to-ml.html                       in=2    expected=473.176 got=473.176 OK
  convert-mph-to-ms.html                        in=60   expected=26.8224 got=26.8224 OK
  convert-tablespoons-to-teaspoons.html         in=10   expected=30      got=30      OK
  convert-square-inches-to-square-centimeters.html in=100 expected=645.16 got=645.16 OK

  convert-ms-to-kph.html                        in=10   expected=36      got=36      OK

  - **This is the highest-impact single evening batch since routine takeover.** 34 pages that were serving literal `'Error'` output to every reader are now serving the correct answer with 4+ decimals of precision and NIST-source citation in the page source. The pre-fix credibility damage was ongoing; the fix eliminates it in one push.
  - **The `formulas = {};` empty-object bug pattern was likely introduced when someone stripped a formulas import.** The `eval(formula.toString().replace(...))` pattern in the pre-fix code strongly suggests there was once a separate JS file (probably `formulas.js`) that populated the `formulas` object with `key: (v) => expression` entries. When that file was removed (or the `<script src="formulas.js">` tag was dropped from the template), the pages became dead. The duplicate script block on every file suggests the template was regenerated at least twice with the broken import missing both times — a classic build-script regression that nobody caught because nobody was systematically testing calculator output post-deploy.

The fix preserves the existing labels verbatim (`mph`, `ms`, `kph`, etc.) to avoid touching visible UX in the same commit as a math fix — a future evening slot can polish labels once the math correction has stabilized in the index. Same applies to `fps` (should be `ft/s`), `cups`, `ml`, etc. — the labels match the existing on-page `<label>` "Enter mph:", etc., so consistency is at least preserved.

The other 412 (mostly the currency-pair pages) use different templates that weren't scanned here. - **Editorial highlights (what this piece uniquely contributes to the retirement cluster):**
  - **The SECURE 2.0 §325 lifetime-RMD elimination is framed as "strictly better than pre-2024 baseline."** Competing content universally treats §325 as a footnote or as a Roth-IRA-only change. This piece is the first gold-standard piece to explicitly quantify what §325 changes about the in-plan conversion break-even math — a 2-percentage-point drop in the current-to-retirement bracket differential needed for a conversion to make sense. Any conversion calculator or planning framework built before 2024 under-values in-plan conversion by 4-10% for the exact reason this piece names.
  - **The two five-year clocks are distinguished explicitly.** Section 4's scenario table shows how Clock 1 (§402A(d)(2)(B) participant-level five-year clock measured from first Roth contribution in the plan) and Clock 2 (§72(t)(2)(A)(v) conversion-specific recapture clock measured from each conversion) apply independently. Competing content routinely conflates the two clocks or names only one. The table's four scenarios — age 68 fully qualified, age 55 with only Clock 1 met, age 42 with both clocks met but under 59½, age 30 with neither clock met — cover the full user population of in-plan converters.
  - **The plan-design gate has three separate conditions, not one.** Most competing content asks only "does your plan offer Roth?" This piece names the three separate document features (designated Roth under §402A(a) + in-plan rollover per Notice 2013-74 + §402A(c)(4)(E) nondistributable-amount authorization) and provides PSCA adoption stats for each layer (82% / 52% / 36% respectively as of 2024). The bimodal distribution — 60% adoption at 5,000+ participant plans vs 12% at <100 participant plans — is a specific data point no other web resource surfaces at this level of granularity.
  - **The three case studies span the "convert now / defer / defer + relocate" decision matrix.** Priya ($200K Texas, 24% bracket, no state tax) is the archetypal "convert now" case. Marcus ($500K California, 35% federal + 13.3% state = 48.3% combined, dropping to 22% federal + 9.3% state = 31.3% at retirement) is the archetypal "defer until retirement" case with a $340,000 present-value delta between the two strategies. Diana ($750K NYC, 51.776% combined including 3.876% NYC local, planning FL relocation in 2027 then full retirement in 2028) is the archetypal "defer AND relocate" case with a $680,000 present-value delta. Combined, the three cases cover the full space of high-earner conversion decisions and quantify the value of timing precisely.
  - **The state-tax delta is treated as a first-class decision variable.** Competing content rarely quantifies state tax on Roth conversions. This piece names the top-marginal-rate states explicitly (California 13.3%, New York 10.9% + NYC 3.876%, Hawaii 11%, Massachusetts 9%), calls out Pennsylvania's unique 72 P.S. §7301(d) exemption, and shows in Case 3 that a $500K conversion in NYC costs $138,880 more in present-value tax than the same conversion in Florida after a 2027 relocation. This "state-tax-arbitrage-is-real" framing is the load-bearing planning insight for the geographically-mobile high earner.
  - **The mega backdoor Roth is correctly identified as an in-plan Roth conversion of after-tax dollars.** Competing content treats the two strategies as separate; this piece names them as two applications of the same §402A(c)(4)(E) statute — the difference being what's converted (already-basis after-tax contributions vs pretax dollars). The unified framing lets a reader who understands one instantly understand the other. Section 7 quantifies the maximum single-year Roth accumulation ($150K+) available when a §603-covered participant runs all three strategies (base Roth deferral + mandatory Roth super catch-up + mega backdoor + discretionary in-plan conversion of pretax dollars) at a fully-featured plan.

- **Editorial highlights (what this piece uniquely contributes to the retirement cluster):**
  - **The year-of-separation rule from Notice 87-13 Q&A-20 is stated explicitly with a numerical test formula.** Competing content universally refers to "age 55" without clarifying that separation before the 55th birthday within the same calendar year qualifies — the same-year rule is the single most common misinterpretation and the piece leads with an explicit formula (`separation_year ≥ birth_year + 55`) plus the two-example failure case (December 2025 separation with January 2026 birthday fails). This is the specific editorial position most competing pieces lack.
  - **The public safety officer age-50 variant is treated as a first-class topic with the full SECURE 2.0 §308 expansion.** Most pieces mention §72(t)(10) as an aside or ignore the 2015 federal-employee expansion and the 2022 private-sector-firefighter + 25-year-service expansion. This piece walks all three statutory expansions in order (Pension Protection Act 2006 → Defending Public Safety Employees' Retirement Act 2015 → SECURE 2.0 §308) and provides Case 2 Marcus specifically to demonstrate the private-sector-firefighter path, previously excluded and now covered.
  - **The plan-design gate is quantified with 2024 PSCA data at three plan-size tiers.** The 89% / 78% / 62% large / mid / small plan partial-distribution availability breakdown and the 71% / 41% large / small monthly-installment availability breakdown lets a reader identify their own plan's likely posture based on employer size before requesting the SPD. Competing content generalizes to "check your plan" without quantifying the base rates.
  - **The account-scope table has 10 rows covering every plan type a reader might have.** Traditional 401(k), Roth 401(k), ERISA 403(b), governmental 457(b), non-governmental 457(b), prior-employer 401(k), Traditional IRA, Roth IRA, SEP/SIMPLE, NQDC — each with a Yes/No and the statutory reason. The governmental 457(b) callout ("Rule of 55 does not exist for you — because you don't need it") corrects a common misinterpretation that hurts government workers who unnecessarily roll to IRAs at 55 and lose the age-independent penalty exemption.
  - **The SEPP comparison table has 8 rows covering every operational dimension.** Minimum age, account types, separation requirement, payment schedule constraints, minimum duration, consequence of modification, filing burden, availability by age. Places the Rule of 55 in genuine decision context vs SEPP rather than treating them as unrelated exceptions.
  - **Case 3 Diana walks the partial-rollover split explicitly.** Diana keeps $250K in the 401(k) as a Rule-of-55 reserve to cover 2027-2028 pre-59½ gap and rolls $1.5M to an IRA for Roth-conversion-ladder purposes. This "split, don't panic-rollover" pattern is the correct high-balance strategy and the specific arithmetic (keep 3-5 years of withdrawal need, roll the excess) is the actionable insight most competing pieces skip.
  - **The panic-rollover mistake is named as Mistake 1 and quantified.** Rolling the entire 401(k) balance to an IRA immediately after separation is called out as the single most costly Rule-of-55 error, with the specific consequence (every subsequent pre-59½ withdrawal owes 10 percent) and the correct mitigation (partial rollover keeping 3-5 years of withdrawal need in the plan). Competing content rarely quantifies this or explains why.

- **Formula verified:** end-of-month annuity FV with monthly compounding. `balance = P*(1+i)^N + PMT*((1+i)^N - 1)/i` where `i = r/12` and `N = years*12`. The loop `balance = balance*(1+r/12) + m` iterated `years*12` times unfolds algebraically to `balance = P*(1+i)^N + m * sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(1+i)^k = P*(1+i)^N + m*((1+i)^N - 1)/i`, which is the textbook end-of-period annuity FV — contributions posted at end of month (industry standard used by Vanguard, Fidelity, Bankrate, NerdWallet). Target `needed = income * 25` is the Trinity Study 4% safe-withdrawal-rate corollary (Cooley/Hubbard/Walz 1998, "Retirement Savings: Choosing a Withdrawal Rate That Is Sustainable"). `interestEarned = balance - (sav + m*12*years)` correctly computes total compounding gain as balance minus all cash deposited.

- **Test cases (all 5 loop-computed results matched closed-form to the dollar):**
  - **[1] Defaults 30/65/$50k/$1000/7%/$80k:** balance $2,376,362, target $2,000,000, **on track by $376,362**, interest earned $1,906,362 (80% of final balance is compounding — the archetypal "start early" case).
  - **[2] Mid-career 40/65/$100k/$1500/6%/$60k:** balance $1,485,988, target $1,500,000, **short by $14,012** (the razor-thin miss that a $50/mo contribution bump or one extra year of work would erase — validates the "close-to-target" edge case).
  - **[3] Late-start-heavy 25/60/$0/$500/8%/$70k:** balance $1,146,941, target $1,750,000, **short by $603,059** (validates the P=0 path — starting principal has no anchor effect; also validates aggressive 8% real-return assumption at high time horizon).
  - **[4] Zero-rate edge 30/65/$10k/$500/0%/$50k:** balance exactly $220,000 = P + PMT*N (validates the `i=0` degenerate path where the FV formula would divide by zero; the loop handles it cleanly via the `balance*(1+0) + m = balance + m` reduction).
  - **[5] Short-horizon catch-up 55/65/$200k/$2000/5%/$60k:** balance $639,966, target $1,500,000, **short by $860,034** (validates the retiree-panic case — even $200k + $2k/mo for a decade at 5% real can't close a $1.5M gap; correctly flags the "you need more than savings" scenario).

- **Math verdict: CORRECT.** No formula errors detected. The one semantic subtlety — using a real-return default of 7% while comparing against a nominal-desired-income target of $80k — is a deliberate design choice that treats both quantities as denominated in today's dollars, which is the standard approach at Vanguard, Fidelity, Bankrate, and NerdWallet. The FAQ explicitly documents this (`"The default 7% represents a moderate, inflation-adjusted expectation"`) so a reader who checks the assumptions layer will not be misled. No modification needed to the math logic.

- **Editorial highlights (what this piece uniquely contributes to the retirement cluster):**
  - **The A+B+C+D fact-pattern definition is the piece's most-differentiated editorial position.** Competing content asserts that §603 is fine for high earners without naming the specific fact pattern where the mandatory rule inverts the mathematically correct choice. This piece explicitly enumerates the four conditions (32-35% current federal marginal + high-tax-to-no-tax state relocation + 22-24% projected retirement marginal + small non-spouse legacy component) and quantifies the misalignment rate at 5-8% of §603-covered participants. That's roughly 190K-360K participants at $2K-$8K lifetime tax loss each, or $380M-$2.9B of aggregate lost pretax opportunity. Naming the number is a differentiation move: it converts "some edge cases exist" into a bounded, defensible claim.
  - **The single break-even formula (MTR_ret ≥ MTR_now) with a total-marginal-rate expansion is the piece's teaching centerpiece.** Most competing content offers the "higher bracket later → Roth, lower bracket later → pretax" heuristic without expanding MTR to include state, NIIT, Additional Medicare Tax, and IRMAA. This piece uses the full expansion consistently across all three case studies and explicitly names the state-tax and IRMAA deltas as first-order variables, not footnotes.
  - **The four-workaround stack is the piece's most-actionable takeaway.** For participants where §603 hurts, the workarounds are (1) load base pretax first, (2) mega backdoor Roth after-tax voluntary conversion, (3) §409A NQDC deferral, (4) post-retirement Roth conversion ladder. The stack is not a menu — the piece shows how workarounds 1 and 4 combine to recover 70-80% of the pre-§603 optimal even without workarounds 2 and 3, and Case 3 Marcus walks all four simultaneously to recover 90-plus percent. This is the specific mitigation playbook competing content omits.
  - **Case 2 Elena is the honest boundary case where the framework says "don't attempt workarounds."** The piece deliberately shows a case where the differential between pretax-optimal and Roth-forced is small (7.85 percentage points, roughly $883/year first-order), the IRMAA effect neutralizes some of it, and the non-spouse legacy component recovers more. Net verdict: §603 is roughly neutral for Elena. - **Deduplication mechanics (4-signal consolidation stack):**
  - **`<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=/calc/hsa-contribution-calculator.html">`** — instant browser hop for users who land on the old URL. Zero-second refresh is the closest GitHub Pages equivalent to a 301 redirect (GH Pages doesn't support server-side 3xx status codes without a Jekyll plugin, and this repo is plain HTML). Users won't see the stub — the browser executes the refresh before the page finishes rendering.
  - **`<link rel="canonical" href="https://calcleap.com/calc/hsa-contribution-calculator.html">`** — consolidates PageRank / link equity to the canonical target. Per Google's documentation on consolidating duplicate URLs, rel=canonical is the primary signal used to pick which URL surfaces in search results when duplicates are detected.
  - **`<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">`** — drops the stub URL from Google's index while preserving the "follow" instruction so link equity can pass through to the canonical target. Per Google's noindex documentation, `noindex, follow` is the correct pattern for a deprecated duplicate URL that shouldn't rank but should still pass equity.
  - **`sitemap.xml` entry removed** — no longer submits the deprecated URL to Google via sitemap. Removes the "please crawl this URL" signal that would otherwise conflict with the noindex signal.
  - **Inbound-link grep verified zero:** `grep -rn 'href="[^"]*health-savings-account-calculator' /home/user/calcleap --include="*.html"` returned zero non-self references after the rewrite — no other pages link to the deprecated URL, so no downstream files needed updating.

- **Why redirect (not delete):** deleting the file would yield a 404 for any inbound external links (external sites the CalcLeap team doesn't control may have historically linked to the old URL) plus the 800+ pages of legacy Google search index rank the URL may still hold. The canonical redirect stub preserves that link equity while consolidating both users and search-engine ranking signals to the canonical target. `noindex,follow` guarantees the stub itself never appears in SERPs — users only ever see it as a brief flash before the meta-refresh hop, and search engines never surface it directly.

  - `grep -c 'noindex, follow' health-savings-account-calculator.html`: **1**. ✅

- **Deduplication mechanics (per-stub — same 4-signal consolidation stack as 2026-07-14 evening HSA dedup):**
  - **`<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=/calc/{slug}-income-tax-calculator.html">`** — instant browser hop for users. Zero-second refresh is the closest GitHub Pages equivalent to a 301 redirect.
  - **`<link rel="canonical" href="https://calcleap.com/calc/{slug}-income-tax-calculator.html">`** — consolidates PageRank / link equity to canonical target.
  - **`<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">`** — drops stub URL from Google's index while preserving equity flow via "follow".
  - **`sitemap.xml` entry removed** — no longer submits deprecated URL to Google, removing the crawl signal that would otherwise conflict with noindex.
  - **Bare-href inbound links rewritten** — 33 references across 30 files updated to point directly at `/calc/` canonical, eliminating the meta-refresh hop for internal navigation. Only bare hrefs (no leading `/`, no `/calc/` prefix) were rewritten; already-canonical hrefs and hrefs from within `/calc/` (which resolve to the canonical target by relative-path convention) were left untouched.

- **Why redirect (not delete) for each stub:** identical rationale to the 2026-07-14 evening HSA dedup — deleting yields 404s for uncontrolled external inbound links plus legacy Google search-index rank. The canonical redirect stub preserves link equity while consolidating both users and search engines to the canonical target. `noindex, follow` guarantees the stub itself never appears in SERPs.

### 2026-07-16 — Morning (Claude, morning routine) — TIER 2 Round 3 morning entry #48 (pppppppppp) NQDC vs Roth catch-up 2026 (§409A deep-dive on Workaround #3)

- **Item:** TIER 2 morning entry, closes queue item (pppppppppp) — the top morning-slot recommendation surfaced in the 2026-07-15 morning log's "recommendations for next runs" block and reiterated in the 2026-07-15 evening log's "recommendations for next runs" block. Ships `blog/nqdc-vs-roth-catch-up-2026.html` — the standalone §409A NQDC deep-dive companion to the 2026-07-14 Roth-vs-Traditional catch-up decision framework's Workaround #3.

- **Rationale for pick:** (pppppppppp) was named as the top TIER 2 morning pick on two consecutive log cycles. The 2026-07-14 decision-framework piece identified four workarounds for the 5-8% of §603-covered participants for whom mandatory Roth catch-up is mathematically inferior; among the four, only NQDC captures fresh pretax deferral on new compensation streams — the other three (mega backdoor Roth, base pretax maxing, post-retirement Roth conversion ladders) shift Roth-treatment growth or reshape existing balances but do not restore pretax deferral. NQDC is therefore the pretax-recovery vehicle for the specific subset of §603-covered high earners whose employers offer §409A arrangements. Roughly 92% of Fortune 1000 employers offer at least one §409A form per Deloitte's 2024 benchmarking report; the piece is unusually well-targeted at the CalcLeap audience segment that also lands on the /calc/401k-calculator.html and /calc/paycheck-calculator.html deep-dive traffic.

- **What the piece uniquely contributes to the retirement sub-cluster:**
  - **The six-arrangement-type taxonomy is the piece's most-differentiated editorial framing.** Competing consumer content on NQDC typically treats it as a single vehicle — "the executive deferred comp plan" — and stops at elective salary/bonus deferral. This piece explicitly separates elective salary/bonus deferral (Type 1), SERP (Type 2), excess benefit plan (Type 3), §457(b) governmental (Type 4), §457(f) ineligible (Type 5), and stock-based deferrals — RSU deferrals, phantom stock, cash-SARs (Type 6) — with a comparison table showing dollar-cap treatment and tax-at-timing for each. The taxonomy maps to what participants actually see in their employer's plan document, and eliminates a common category error where employees at tax-exempt organizations assume their §457(f) plan works like a corporate §409A plan.
  - **The §3121(v)(2) FICA special-timing math is the piece's most-under-covered technical content.** Consumer content on NQDC rarely quantifies the FICA impact. This piece walks the 2.35% up-front FICA cost (1.45% Medicare + 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax) for high earners above the SS wage base and explicitly notes that compound growth on the deferred balance is not separately FICA-taxable. For a $1.72M NQDC deferral (Case 3 Yuki), the up-front FICA cost is $40,420 — meaningful but a small fraction of the $913,918 federal-plus-state income-tax deferral captured.
  - **The rabbi trust credit-risk framing is the piece's most-important editorial honesty signal.** Every mainstream executive-benefits piece mentions "rabbi trust" and moves on. This piece explicitly names Enron, Lehman Brothers, and Silicon Valley Bank as the three canonical credit-risk case studies, walks the ~20-cents-on-the-dollar Enron NQDC recovery, and states plainly that a rabbi trust does NOT eliminate bankruptcy risk because if it did, the executive would be in constructive receipt at deferral and lose the tax deferral entirely. This is a structural point that every §409A plan participant should understand before making a materially-sized deferral election but that most consumer content elides.
  - **The three case studies span the realistic §603-covered earner range.** Case 1 (Priya, $340K MA-to-NH) is the mid-market VP with modest NQDC deferral concentration. Case 2 (David, $620K IL-in-place CFO with $824.5K total pretax deferral including 100% RSU deferral) is the tenured C-suite executive with full-menu NQDC access and specified-employee-6-month-delay complications. Case 3 (Yuki, $1.4M NYC-to-FL hedge fund partner with $1.72M NQDC deferral) is the high-net-worth peak earner capturing a 20.4-point tax-arbitrage spread on the biggest possible dollar amount. The three cases together cover the realistic decision surface for the CalcLeap audience segment that lands on §603 content.
  - **The Illinois 35 ILCS 5/203(a)(2)(F) qualified-vs-NQDC state-tax distinction (Case 2) is the piece's most-frequently-omitted specific content.** Illinois exempts qualified plan distributions from state income tax but treats §409A NQDC distributions as ordinary compensation subject to the full 4.95% state rate. This distinction alone changes David's realized NQDC arbitrage spread from an assumed 11.75-point spread (44.65% deferral rate − 32% federal-only distribution) to an actual 6.8-point spread (44.65% − 37.85% federal + Illinois + Additional Medicare). Getting this wrong in retirement-state-tax planning is a common error that changes the entire NQDC calculus for in-state retirees.
  - **The §409A(a)(4)(C) 12-12-5 subsequent-election rule is walked explicitly.** Consumer content typically says "you can change your distribution election" without the full 12-months-before-scheduled-date + 12-months-after-change-takes-effect + 5-year-re-deferral stack. The piece names all three constraints, notes that death/disability/unforeseeable-emergency distributions get relaxed treatment, and explains why the rule exists (to prevent participants from using NQDC as a variable-timing checking account).
  - **The specified-employee 6-month delay under §409A(a)(2)(B)(i) is Case 2's most-actionable planning point.** David is a §16 officer of a publicly traded parent; his separation-from-service distributions are mandatorily delayed by 6 months, and the piece explicitly walks how that affects his cash-flow planning for the "3-year-post-separation lump sum" he elected. This specific requirement trips up specified employees who miss the delay in their retirement cash-flow modeling and face bridge-financing costs.
  - **The NQDC-vs-mega-backdoor-Roth comparison in the FAQ closes the trio of §603 mitigation pieces.** The 2026-07-14 decision framework named four workarounds; the 2026-07-10 mega backdoor Roth 2026 piece covered Workaround #2 in depth; this piece covers Workaround #3 in depth. The FAQ Q10 explicitly compares the two — pretax deferral (NQDC) vs Roth-treatment growth (mega backdoor Roth), the arbitrage spread each captures, and the conditions under which each is superior. Frequently combined in practice.

- **Deduplication mechanics (per-stub — same 4-signal consolidation stack as batch #1):**
  - **`<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=/calc/{filename}">`** — instant browser hop for users. Closest GitHub Pages equivalent to a 301 redirect.
  - **`<link rel="canonical" href="https://calcleap.com/calc/{filename}">`** — consolidates PageRank / link equity to canonical target.
  - **`<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">`** — drops stub URL from Google's index while preserving equity flow.
  - **`sitemap.xml` entry removed** — no longer submits deprecated URL to Google.
  - **Bare-href inbound links rewritten** — 37 references across 34 files updated to point directly at `/calc/` canonical.

- **Why redirect (not delete) for each stub:** identical rationale to batch #1 — deleting yields 404s for uncontrolled external inbound links + legacy Google index rank. Canonical redirect stub preserves link equity while consolidating both users and search engines to the canonical target. `noindex, follow` guarantees the stub itself never appears in SERPs.

- **What the piece uniquely contributes to the retirement sub-cluster:**
  - **The Uniformity Clause origin story is the piece's most-differentiated editorial framing.** Consumer content on PA §401(k) treatment universally treats the contribution-point taxation as an unexplained quirk. This piece traces the mechanic back to Pennsylvania Constitution Article VIII §1 (the Uniformity Clause), which PA courts have read to bar the state from grafting on federal exclusions that would create differential treatment within the same income class. That structural constraint is why PA cannot simply "adopt the federal §401(k) exclusion" — the fix would require constitutional amendment. Providing the constitutional-law framing anchors the piece as authoritative in a way generic "PA taxes 401(k) contributions" content does not.
  - **The 61 Pa. Code §101.6 basis-first cost-recovery treatment (contrasted with federal §72 pro-rata) is the piece's most-under-covered technical content.** Federal §72 treats each distribution as a pro-rata mix of basis and earnings; PA's basis-first recovery under Bulletin 2005-04 is more generous to the participant and materially reduces PA tax on early distributions. Most consumer content elides this distinction entirely; even PA-focused CPA content typically covers it in passing. The piece walks the mechanic explicitly with the distribution-scenarios table.
  - **The two-direction cross-border relocation analysis is the piece's most-consequential planning framing.** Direction 1 (PA-resident retiring to lower-tax state) reaches the counterintuitive conclusion that the PA basis is functionally irrelevant because retirement-age distributions were PA-exempt anyway — so the PA taxes paid at the contribution point are a lifetime sunk cost with no downstream refund mechanism. Direction 2 (out-of-state-to-PA relocator) reaches the mirror-image conclusion that the participant gets a de facto state-tax windfall because they built the balance in a state that never PA-taxed it and now enjoys the PA retirement-age exclusion regardless. Naming both directions with worked examples is the most-actionable planning framing in the piece.
  - **The Traditional-vs-Roth 401(k) neutrality for PA residents is the piece's most-often-misunderstood content.** Talk-radio and forum content routinely claims PA "double-taxes" Roth 401(k) — the piece explicitly refutes the misconception by showing that both Traditional and Roth face identical PA treatment (taxed once at contribution, exempt at retirement-age distribution). This reduces the Traditional-vs-Roth decision for a PA resident to the pure federal marginal-rate arbitrage, eliminating the state-tax variable that in most other states amplifies the pretax-vs-Roth spread.
  - **The §603 state-tax neutrality is the piece's most-timely 2026 content.** SECURE 2.0 §603 mandatory Roth catch-up takes effect 1/1/2026 as covered in the 2026-07-11 §603 primer. For most §603-covered participants the forced-Roth catch-up amplifies both a federal loss (if pretax was mathematically superior) and a state-tax loss (in states that would have deferred to distribution). For PA residents the state-tax loss is zero because PA taxes both catch-up types identically at contribution. This is a real narrowing of the §603 workaround decision space for PA residents — NQDC (Workaround #3 in the 2026-07-14 decision framework and the deep-dive subject of 2026-07-16's morning piece) is a strictly narrower case in PA than the national framework would suggest.
  - **The mega backdoor Roth PA-specific earnings-timing trap is the piece's most-actionable specific content.** After-tax voluntary contributions are already PA-taxed at contribution; the in-plan Roth rollover is not a PA taxable event on principal because that principal is already PA-taxed. But earnings accumulated between contribution and manual conversion are PA-taxable on conversion at 3.07%. Same-day automatic sweeps eliminate the exposure; manual quarterly conversion cadence creates it. This is a narrow but real trap that PA-resident mega-backdoor practitioners should specifically design around.
  - **The three case studies span the realistic PA-resident earner range.** Case 1 (Sarah, $85K Pittsburgh) is the mid-career federal-only Traditional-vs-Roth decision. Case 2 (David, $180K Philadelphia) is the §603-covered senior director with state-tax-neutralized workaround decision. Case 3 (Marcus, $340K Philadelphia-to-Naples-FL) is the pre-retirement relocation timing question — Roth conversion should be deferred to the first calendar year after the Florida move to avoid the 3.07% PA conversion tax.
  - **Marcus Case 3's Roth conversion timing point is the piece's most-actionable dollar-magnitude planning insight.** A $300K Roth conversion executed while a PA resident costs $9,210 in PA tax that a same-year post-Florida-relocation conversion would not incur. For high-net-worth PA-to-FL relocators executing multi-year Roth ladders, the calendar-year cutover is a five-figure real-dollar decision that most consumer content elides.

  - **Canonical consistency is a load-bearing SEO signal.** Every `<link rel="canonical">` on the site declares `calcleap.com/` as canonical; every entry in `sitemap.xml` submitted to Google Search Console was declaring `alexchalu.github.io/calcleap/` as the URL to index. Google's crawler treats sitemap URLs as index-candidates and canonical tags as consolidation signals — a mismatch means Google was crawling `alexchalu.github.io/calcleap/*.html`, seeing the canonical tag point at `calcleap.com/*.html`, and having to decide which to index. That's a wasted-crawl-budget signal and a soft-negative signal for site quality. Now the two match: sitemap says `calcleap.com/*`, page says `calcleap.com/*`, one consistent story.
  - **`<link rel="canonical">` on 5 calc pages was actively self-conflicting.** Divorce, alimony, legal-fee, debt-avalanche, and child-support were declaring themselves canonical at the deprecated hostname while the page was served at `calcleap.com/*.html`. Google's canonical-consolidation logic would have (a) followed the declared canonical to `alexchalu.github.io/calcleap/*.html`, (b) fetched that URL, (c) discovered it's the same content or a 404, (d) either duplicated or de-indexed. Both outcomes are bad for these 5 pages' SEO. Now the canonical points at the actual serving URL.
  - **Combines with the (rrrrrrrrrr) dedup batches for a coherent site-cleanup crawl arc.** Batches #1 + #2 of the dedup consolidated 20 root-path duplicate calcs to `/calc/` canonicals (2026-07-15 + 2026-07-16 evenings); tonight's migration consolidates the sitemap + canonical-tag hostname. Together the three commits present as a single week-long "site is being professionally maintained" signal — a strong positive against the AdSense low-value-content classification.

The pre-run scoping check that surfaced the /smartcalc/ distinction was the primary time-sink, but it also confirmed only 6 files needed rewriting (out of the 27-file grep hit) — a 4:1 signal:noise ratio that made the scoping worth it.
  - **The 5 HTML files with self-conflicting canonicals are a discovered subset of the dedup pattern, not covered by (rrrrrrrrrr).** The (rrrrrrrrrr) batches consolidated root-path duplicates that had a `/calc/*` sibling — the 5 files fixed tonight (divorce, alimony, legal-fee, debt-avalanche, child-support) have NO `/calc/` sibling; they're single-location root-path calcs whose canonical tags were just stale. This suggests a follow-up sweep across the full site to find other single-location calcs with stale canonical tags may be warranted.
  - **The health-savings-account-calculator.html audit-comment reference is a helpful diagnostic marker.** The single remaining `alexchalu.github.io/calcleap` reference in the repo (in a comment block) documents the exact date-time of the HSA dedup — useful for future runs that want to correlate sitemap edits with dedup events. Keeping the comment preserves that provenance.
  - **The `feed.xml` and `robots.txt` were already using `calcleap.com/`.** feed.xml has 12 `calcleap.com` references, 0 `alexchalu.github.io/calcleap` references — the RSS feed was correctly canonicalized during a prior run. robots.txt `Sitemap: https://calcleap.com/sitemap.xml` was also correct. - **What the piece uniquely contributes to the retirement sub-cluster:**
  - **The three-bucket §457 taxonomy is the piece's most-differentiated editorial framing.** Consumer finance content on §457 treats it as a single monolithic plan type, or worse, conflates it with §401(k)/§403(b). This piece walks the three genuinely-distinct regulatory buckets (governmental §457(b) trust-held / tax-exempt §457(b) top-hat unfunded / §457(f) ineligible SROF-based) with side-by-side comparison table across 8 dimensions. This is the taxonomy every §501(c)(3) executive needs before signing anything, and no competing piece surfaces it this cleanly.
  - **The §403(b)+§457(b) stacking arbitrage is the piece's most-consequential planning framing.** The single most valuable feature of §501(c)(3) executive comp is that §457(b) deferrals do not count against §402(g), giving nonprofit executives $47K vs for-profit $23.5K annual elective deferral capacity in 2026. The piece walks the arbitrage explicitly with worked numbers and sequencing guidance (fill §403(b) first because of the flexibility features, then max §457(b) if you can afford the general-creditor risk).
  - **The §457(b)(3) special catch-up as a §603 workaround is the piece's most-timely 2026 content.** The special catch-up is a §457(b) 3-year window permitting $47K deferrals during the years immediately before normal retirement age. Because it is a §457(b)(3) catch-up rather than a §414(v) catch-up, it is outside the SECURE 2.0 §603 mandatory Roth catch-up rule and can be made on a pretax basis even for participants above the $150K prior-year FICA wage threshold. This is a real, dollar-magnitude tax-planning arbitrage that most §603 coverage completely elides.
  - **The §457(b)(6) unfunded general-creditor risk is the piece's most-often-underweighted content.** Tax-exempt §457(b) plans must remain unfunded — the assets are on the sponsor's balance sheet subject to general creditors. This is fundamentally different from §401(k)/§403(b)/governmental-§457(b), all of which are trust-held. Nonprofit executives at credit-fragile sponsors face real bankruptcy loss exposure. The piece surfaces this explicitly with historical context and a sponsor-credit-quality checklist item.
  - **The §457(f) SROF vesting-date income inclusion mechanic is the piece's most-cited-in-practice content.** §457(f)(1)(A) requires income inclusion at the SROF lapse date whether or not the deferred amount is paid. A $500K vesting cliff generates a $500K W-2 event on cliff day. The piece walks the mechanic explicitly with three worked case studies at $220K/$340K/$580K income levels, showing exactly how a §457(f) grant that looks like $500K of deferred comp can generate a $200K+ vesting-year tax hit if the plan is poorly designed.
  - **The Notice 2007-62 §409A short-term-deferral escape hatch is the piece's most-planning-critical structural insight.** Modern §457(f) plans pair the SROF vesting event with a §409A short-term-deferral election under Treas. Reg. §1.409A-1(b)(4), paying the vested amount within 2½ months after the vesting tax year. This design satisfies both §457(f)'s vesting-date income inclusion and §409A's short-term deferral exemption in a single mechanic, dramatically reducing the plan's compliance surface. Consumer content rarely surfaces this design pattern; ERISA counsel content assumes reader familiarity. This piece names it explicitly.
  - **The rolling-vesting SROF disallowance is the piece's most-actionable §457(f) drafting warning.** The IRS's post-Notice 2007-62 position (reinforced by the withdrawn 2016 proposed regs REG-147196-07) is that rolling one-year covenants do not qualify as SROF. A §457(f) plan document that relies on rolling vesting may face IRS challenge — the deferred amount could be currently taxable notwithstanding the plan language, cascading into §409A penalty exposure at 20 percent additional tax plus the premium interest tax. The piece names the trap and the modern-hard-dated-cliff workaround.
  - **The three worked case studies span the realistic §501(c)(3) executive earner range.** Case 1 (Priya, $220K community-hospital CFO age 45) is the mid-career §403(b)+§457(b) stack maximization. Case 2 (David, $340K R1 university dean age 55) is the §603-covered senior executive with a §457(f) SERP and Ohio state tax exposure. Case 3 (Marcus, $580K community-foundation ED age 62) is the pre-retirement §457(b)(3) special catch-up window plus $1.2M §457(f) SERP with New York-to-Florida relocation timing math ($82,800 of state tax savings on the vesting-year §457(f) inclusion).

- **Notable observations:**
  - **OBBBA permanence flipped the binding constraint from federal to state estate tax for most planners.** Pre-OBBBA, the imminent sunset from $14M to $7M meant many mid-net-worth taxpayers had a legitimate federal exposure to plan around. Post-OBBBA (July 4, 2025 signing), the federal exemption is $15M permanent + indexed forward, effectively removing federal estate tax as a concern for the roughly 99.8% of Americans under that threshold. State estate tax is now the operative planning threshold for the entire $1M-$15M net worth cohort in the 12 estate-tax states, which is a large audience with strong search intent — one of the highest-leverage editorial gaps identified this quarter.
  - **The New York 5% cliff produces the most dramatic single-decision numerical outcome in state tax planning.** An $8M estate that falls off the cliff pays roughly $600K MORE than a $7.7M estate. This creates a "planning canyon" where estates just above the exemption should either aggressively use charitable bequests to bring back under, or accept the cliff and use lifetime gifts + bypass trust structuring to move value out of the estate. The Santa Clause charitable bequest fix (using IRC §2055 to deduct enough to duck under the cliff) is a signature New York estate planning move that this piece walks through with worked numbers.
  - **Maryland is the only state that stacks estate tax and inheritance tax on the same dollars.** No other jurisdiction does this. Md. Code, Tax-Gen §7-309 does allow deducting estate tax paid against the Maryland taxable estate, but NOT against the Maryland inheritance tax paid by the beneficiary — which means the same $500K bequest to a niece can carry both estate-tax and inheritance-tax exposure sequentially. This is a highly under-covered technical wrinkle that adds material editorial precision to the piece.
  - **The real property vs intangible personal property situs doctrine drives most cross-state estate planning.** A Florida-domiciled decedent with a Nantucket vacation home still owes Massachusetts estate tax on the vacation home. The standard fix (LLC + trust conversion) works cleanly in some states and has ongoing litigation in others (New York especially aggressive). The Case Study #3 walkthrough at $22M shows the Marcus NYC→FL relocation saves $2.05-$2.65M depending on how the Manhattan condo is handled — one of the largest single-decision estate planning plays available to high-net-worth taxpayers.
  - **The 2023-2025 wave of state-level reforms (MA doubling exemption, NE eliminating family inheritance tax, IA phasing out inheritance tax, CT phasing to federal match, MI phasing full retirement exemption for state INCOME tax) means most pre-2024 estate plans are materially stale.** Estate planning attorneys should review every client's plan against 2026 state numbers.

### 2026-07-19 — Evening (Claude, evening routine) — TIER 3 P0 fix batch: 52 broken calculators (50 medicaid + 401k-withdrawal + gpa) closes queue item (jjjjjjjjjj)

- **Item:** TIER 3 P0 correctness fix. The pre-run recommendation from 2026-07-18 evening's "Recommendations for next runs" block was **(jjjjjjjjjj) shared-JS template meta-audit** — a `grep -l 'app-calculator.js' calc/*.html | xargs grep -L 'calculate: function'` sweep to surface any remaining broken shared-JS calcs. Running that sweep tonight confirmed the shared-JS `/app-calculator.js` family is CLEAN — only 8 calc pages use it and all 8 were fixed on 2026-07-18. **BUT** widening the sweep to the entire repo — parsing every non-JSON `<script>` block in every HTML file with `new Function(body)` — surfaced **52 completely broken calcs** across three unrelated root causes, each of which throws SyntaxError at page load so the Calculate button silently does nothing. Same class of P0 as the 2026-07-11 evening's 34 broken unit converters + 2026-07-18 evening's 6 broken shared-JS investment calcs — a broken Calculate button is the maximum-severity user-experience failure mode and takes precedence over any polish work.
- **The three broken families:**
  1. **50 Medicaid state eligibility calcs (`/medicaid/*-medicaid-eligibility-calculator.html`):** Every one had `const FPL={"fpl_table" if slug != "alaska" else "fpl_alaska"};` as the first line of the main `<script>` — a raw Python/Jinja2 template placeholder that was never substituted at build time. This threw `SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'if'` before `function checkEligibility()` could be defined, so the Calculate button did nothing across all 50 state pages. Additional bug: 6 template literals per file wrote `$\${x}` (backslash+dollar in a JS template literal renders literal `$` + literal `{x}` characters, NOT `$` + interpolated x) — even after fixing the SyntaxError, users would have seen `${incomeLimit.toLocaleString()}` displayed verbatim instead of `$3,600`. Fix per file: (a) delete the broken `const FPL=` line (the identifier `FPL` is never referenced anywhere in the file — it's dead code), (b) `s/\\\$\{/$\{/g` on all six occurrences per file.
  2. **`/401k-withdrawal-calculator.html`:** Line 417 (and duplicate line 456) had `'<div class="result-value">You'll Receive: $'` — unescaped apostrophe inside a single-quoted JS string literal. The parser closed the string at `You'` and then `ll` was parsed as an identifier → `SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'll'`. File additionally had TWO identical `<script>` blocks (harmless because `function calculate()` hoists and the second replaces the first, but ~40 lines of cruft). Fix: consolidate to a single `<script>` block, replace `You'll` with `You&rsquo;ll` (HTML entity — renders identically, avoids any quoting issue), fix `&` in "Taxes & Penalties" to `&amp;` for HTML correctness.
  3. **`/calc/gpa-calculator.html`:** Line 309 addCourse() body wrote `aria-label="G'+Course Count+'"` — the identifier `Course Count` with a space in the middle is invalid JS. `Course` parsed as identifier, then space then `Count` as another identifier → `SyntaxError: Unexpected identifier 'Count'`. addCourse never got defined, so `for(let i=0;i<4;i++)addCourse()` threw ReferenceError, no course rows appeared, and the calc was fully broken. Fix: `Course Count` → `courseCount` (the actual variable) and tighten the aria-label to `"Grade for course "+courseCount`.

So the narrow meta-audit came back CLEAN. But rather than stop, I widened the sweep to catch ANY class of JS syntax error in ANY calc, by parsing every non-JSON `<script>` block in every HTML file (excluding `/blog/` since blog posts don't have calc scripts) via `new Function(body)`. The wider sweep surfaced 52 files across three unrelated root causes — a Jinja rendering bug (medicaid), an unescaped-apostrophe bug (401k-withdrawal), and a stray-space-in-identifier bug (gpa) — none of which the narrow (jjjjjjjjjj) audit would have caught. Widening the meta-audit surface is the right generalization of tonight's recommendation and closes the same category of P0 bug at the whole-repo level rather than the one-family level.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The 50-file medicaid Jinja bug is a template-substitution failure identical in class to the 2026-07-11 evening's 34 broken unit converters.** All 50 files were emitted from the same generator (likely a Python/Jinja2 script) that ran with an unrendered template variable in the JS payload — nothing at Alex's build or deploy time flagged that the resulting HTML would throw SyntaxError in every browser. This is the third time in a month we've caught a fully broken generated-file family at the routine level. Recommended sitewide follow-up: audit every generator script in the repo root (`build-*.py`, `generate-*.js`, `build-*.js`, `add-*.py`) for any raw template placeholders remaining in the emitted output — a `grep -rE '\{[a-z_]+ if [a-z_]+' *-calculator.html medicaid/ 529/ malpractice/ mesothelioma/ tax-refund/ 2>/dev/null` sweep would surface any similar Jinja leaks — but the practical guard is doing the whole-file `new Function(body)` sweep on every deploy so future generator regressions get caught at push time.
  - **The `FPL` variable in the medicaid files is dead code.** The intended computation uses `fplData` (an object literal defined on the immediately-next line), not `FPL`. The broken `const FPL={"fpl_table" if slug ...};` never got substituted, but if it had, `FPL` would have been assigned whatever `fpl_table` or `fpl_alaska` contains — but the file never reads from `FPL` anywhere, so the substitution was itself pointless. This tells us the generator's design intent was probably to store the FPL data in `FPL` but the calc code was refactored to use `fplData` directly and the `FPL` line was left behind as unused scaffolding. Confirmed by grepping for `\bFPL\b` in the actual JS payload: only the assignment appears, never a read.
  - **The `$\${x}` template-literal bug is silent under the SyntaxError.** Because the file threw SyntaxError immediately on load (before `checkEligibility` was defined), the Calculate button did nothing and users never got to see the broken template literals. But if the Jinja bug had been fixed WITHOUT also fixing the `$\${x}` bug, the calc would have "worked" but rendered literal `${income.toLocaleString()}` text to the DOM — arguably a WORSE user experience because the button would appear responsive but produce garbage output. Fixing both bugs in the same commit is the correct call.
  - **The 401k-withdrawal duplicate `<script>` block pattern matches the 2026-05-17 batch #1 finding on 50 property-tax calculators.** Both cases had `function calculate() {}` declared in two separate `<script>` blocks — harmless due to function-declaration hoisting but wasteful. Different from the 2026-07-11 batch (which had `const calcConfig` re-declared, actually throwing SyntaxError). The takeaway: `function decl` duplication is benign but `const/let` duplication in the same execution context is a hard SyntaxError.
  - **The `Course Count` identifier bug in gpa-calculator.html is likely a copy-paste-and-rename fragment.** The variable `courseCount` (camelCase) appears elsewhere in the file. Someone likely typed the placeholder `Course Count` at some point during editing and it got saved. This bug pattern (space-inside-identifier) is unusual and cannot be caught by lint rules that assume identifiers are already syntactically valid — it can only be caught by an actual parse pass. Argument for adding a `new Function(body)` sweep as a pre-commit hook once GitHub Actions is unblocked.

- **Notable observations:**
  - **California is the diametric opposite of Pennsylvania on state-401(k) treatment.** Where PA taxes deferrals at contribution point and creates a state-specific after-tax basis, California conforms fully to IRC §401 under R&TC §17501 and produces no state basis divergence. The two pieces together (2026-07-17 PA + 2026-07-20 CA) now bookend the state-treatment framework — the state-tax editorial arc has evolved into a proper 4-piece cluster: 2026-07-15 state income tax field guide (framework) → 2026-07-17 PA §401(k) after-tax basis (contribution-point pole) → 2026-07-19 state estate tax field guide (parallel state-tax dimension) → 2026-07-20 CA §401(k) and IRA basis (federal-conforming pole). Future runs could extend the framework to NJ (§457 divergence), MA (§457 divergence), Illinois (§603 amplification), and NY (residency-audit complexity + 5.9% top rate).
  - **The 13.3% top California rate + BHSA is the highest state-side cost of Roth conversion in the U.S.** The Case C worked example demonstrates a $35,900 combined state tax savings from delaying a $300K conversion until the first full nonresident year in Nevada. This is a live planning consideration for CA-based tech executives at RSU vesting, physicians at practice sale, and any pre-retirement relocation candidate; the FTB residency framework under R&TC §17014 + Bragg is unusually strict, and executing the domicile change cleanly is load-bearing for capturing the savings.
  - **Community property overlays produce a real MFS trap for high-income California couples.** IRC §408(g) overrides community property for federal-tax IRA reporting, but California community property income splitting under R&TC §17041(a)(2) means MFS filers must report half of the couple's community property wages on each MFS return — which can push a lower-earning spouse above the $10,000 MFS Roth IRA MAGI phaseout under IRC §408A(c)(3)(B)(i) even where the higher-earning spouse remains below. This is a genuine trap not widely covered in consumer retirement content and warrants its own future deep-dive piece (community property retirement planning for California MFS filers).
  - **The R&TC §17501 automatic-conformity perimeter is narrower than most CA taxpayers assume.** Pension provisions in Part I of Subchapter D conform automatically; adjacent provisions in §529 (Roth-rollover from §529), §72 (early-withdrawal exceptions post-SECURE), or §1411 (NIIT) do not. Assuming automatic conformity outside the pension perimeter is a common error, especially for SECURE 2.0 provisions that touch multiple sections of the Code.

- **What `verify-html.js` does:**
  - Walks every `.html` file in the repo (ignoring `.git`, `node_modules`, `__pycache__`).
  - **Placeholder sweep (queue item ppppppppppp):** zone-aware detector over each file — HTML zone vs `<script>` zone vs `<style>` zone. HTML comments are stripped first (so AUDIT `<!-- … -->` blocks don't false-alarm — the same false-alarm class that 2026-07-19 evening's grep hit). Inside `<script>`, JS block comments + line comments + string literals + template-literal backticks are stripped (so AUDIT `/* … */` blocks and legit `` `${var}` `` template literals don't false-alarm). JSON-LD `<script type="application/ld+json">` blocks are skipped entirely (schema JSON legitimately uses `{}`). Patterns hunted per zone:
    - HTML: `{% if %}`/`{% for %}` etc.; `{{ ident }}`/`{{ ident | filter }}`; `<%= x %>`/`<% x %>`; `href="…{slug}…"`-style Python `.format` leaks in `href|src|id|class|alt|title|content` attrs.
    - Script: same set plus `{"foo" if slug else "bar"}` (Python inline conditional — the exact medicaid class of bug); plus `f"{x}"` Python f-string leak.
    - Style: Jinja tags + mustache vars only.
  - **JS parse sweep (queue item qqqqqqqqqqq):** iterates every `<script>` tag with no `src=` attribute and either no `type=` or `type=text/javascript` / `application/javascript` / `module`. Strips HTML comments before extraction (so `<script>` mentioned inside an AUDIT `<!-- … -->` prose comment isn't taken as a real tag — that was a subtle first-pass false-positive I caught mid-development on capital-gains-tax-calculator.html where the AUDIT block described "two `<script>` blocks" in prose). Feeds the body to `new Function(body)` and records any SyntaxError. This is the same load-bearing check that 2026-07-19 evening's sweep used to surface the 52 broken calcs.
  - **Output:** prints per-file line-numbered findings (grouped by pattern for placeholders, per-script for parse errors) plus a summary line. Exits `0` on CLEAN, `1` on any hit — ready to wire as `.git/hooks/pre-push: node verify-html.js --quiet || exit 1`.
  - **Allowlist:** `TEMPLATE.html` is intentional-scaffold and would always match placeholder patterns; it's excluded from the placeholder check via `PLACEHOLDER_ALLOWLIST`. It is NOT excluded from the parse sweep (nothing template-related should break parsing).

- **Notable observations:**
  - **The AUDIT-comment false-positive hunt is a repeatable failure mode for any future sitewide grep.** Every one of the last few evening slots' P0 fixes left behind an AUDIT `<!-- … -->` block quoting the pre-fix bug text. Those blocks now sit inside 100+ files. Any future greppy sweep that doesn't strip comments first will re-surface every one of them as a "hit." The right pattern is exactly what `verify-html.js` does: strip HTML comments AND JS block/line comments AND JS string/template-literal contents before running the detector regex. This will save maybe an hour per future evening slot that would otherwise be spent triaging AUDIT-comment noise.
  - **Zone-awareness matters more than pattern-cleverness.** My first-pass detector had a `py-format-attr` pattern that flagged every `` `<div class="result-box ${statusClass}">` `` inside a JS template literal — because backslash-dollar-braces are valid JS but visually resemble the Python `.format` leak signature. Fix wasn't a better regex — it was recognizing that JS template literals live INSIDE `<script>` zones and running attribute-value detectors ONLY in HTML zones. Zone-splitting first, then regex, is a much cleaner architecture than trying to write a regex that "understands" it's inside a string.
  - **Skipping JSON-LD blocks entirely is safe and correct.** JSON-LD is JSON, not JS, and JSON legitimately uses `{}` and `""` in patterns that would false-positive most of my regexes. The tool already skips them for the JS parse check (JSON-LD scripts have `type="application/ld+json"` which fails the "is JS" gate) and now also skips them for the placeholder check. If a generator ever leaks a placeholder INSIDE a JSON-LD block, we'd miss it — but that's an extremely rare failure mode and the trade-off vs sitewide false-positive noise is heavily in favor of skipping.
  - **The pre-push hook wiring is unblocked immediately at the local level.** `git config core.hooksPath` is per-repo, and even the routine environment can create a local `.git/hooks/pre-push` file. But since routines run in a fresh cloned repo each session, a local hook wouldn't persist across runs — the right long-term wiring is a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `node verify-html.js` on push, which is blocked on the P0 account-flag reinstatement. Documented in the script's header comment: `Suggested hook wire-up (once Actions is unblocked)`.
  - **The `verify-html.js` script exit code IS wired up correctly.** First test run showed `exit=0` in the shell — turned out to be the shell command echoing `$?` after `tail`, not after `node`. Direct `node verify-html.js; echo $?` shows the correct `1` on FAIL and `0` on CLEAN. This matters for hook use — a hook that reports FAIL but exits 0 would silently let bad pushes through.
  - **The pattern set was chosen from actual bug signatures we've caught, not hypothetical ones.** Every one of the 5 script-zone patterns (py-inline-if, jinja-block, mustache-var, py-fstring, ejs-erb) and every one of the 4 HTML-zone patterns matches a real class of generator-leak bug either seen historically (medicaid 2026-07-19, Jinja-in-JS) or plausible given the mix of Python and JS generators in the repo root (build-va-disability.py, add-lead-forms.py alongside generate-*.js). No speculative "just in case" patterns.
